choices: Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY — the alias doesn't exist yet at WHERE time; repeat the expression or wrap in a subquery/CTE
Aliases work everywhere; the error is a bug in SQL Server
Move the alias to the FROM clause
Use the alias in GROUP BY instead
evidence: SELECT price * qty AS line_total FROM order_items WHERE line_total > 100;
scenarios.hint: Which clause runs first — WHERE, or SELECT?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the alias fail in WHERE?
scenarios.situation: A query filters on a SELECT alias and gets 'Invalid column name'. The same alias works in ORDER BY.
scenarios.title: The alias that wasn't there
scenarios.why: SQL's logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. WHERE executes before the SELECT list, so the alias doesn't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after, so it does. Fix: repeat the expression in WHERE, or wrap the query (CTE/subquery) so the alias becomes a real column in the outer scope.

choices: OFFSET/FETCH (or keyset pagination) — OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY; keyset (WHERE id > last_seen) is stable under concurrent inserts
TOP 20 with a page-number variable — TOP skips pages automatically
ROW_NUMBER() in the WHERE clause directly
OFFSET without ORDER BY — order doesn't matter for pages
evidence:
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY product_id
OFFSET 40 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;
scenarios.hint: What happens to page 3 when 5 new rows land at the top while the user is on page 2?
scenarios.prompt: What are the pagination options, and what is OFFSET's weakness?
scenarios.situation: A product listing paginates with OFFSET/FETCH. Users report seeing duplicate items across pages during busy periods.
scenarios.title: The shifting pages
scenarios.why: OFFSET counts rows from the current result start — concurrent inserts/deletes shift everything, causing duplicates/skips across pages. OFFSET/FETCH is simple and fine for static data. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > @last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n) is stable under churn and faster on deep pages (no scanning skipped rows). Choose by data volatility.

choices: UNION ALL — keeps duplicates, no sort/dedupe pass; use UNION only when dedup is required
UNION is faster because it sorts
They are identical; UNION is shorter to type
UNION ALL removes duplicates
scenarios.hint: Which one pays for a sort-and-dedupe pass you may not need?
scenarios.prompt: Which set operator, and why does the choice matter?
scenarios.situation: Two regional sales tables are combined for a yearly report. Regions never overlap, so no row can appear in both.
scenarios.title: The combined report
scenarios.why: UNION performs a distinct-sort to remove duplicates — expensive and pointless when the sets are disjoint. UNION ALL concatenates without dedup: faster and preserves true duplicates when they matter. Default to UNION ALL; reach for UNION only when deduplication is semantically required.

choices: NULL comparisons need IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE; the predicate silently excludes NULLs
NULL = NULL is TRUE in SQL Server
Add an index on the column
Use COALESCE in the JOIN condition
evidence: SELECT * FROM tickets WHERE resolved_by = NULL; -- 0 rows, but unresolved tickets exist
scenarios.hint: What does '= NULL' evaluate to — TRUE, FALSE, or something else?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the query return zero rows?
scenarios.situation: A 'find unresolved tickets' query uses resolved_by = NULL and returns nothing, though unresolved tickets exist.
scenarios.title: The NULL comparison
scenarios.why: SQL uses three-valued logic: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. '= NULL' never matches — use IS NULL. The same trap: NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns nothing. Internalize it: NULL isn't a value, it's the absence of one; only IS NULL / IS NOT NULL / COALESCE test it.

choices: LIKE with ESCAPE for the literal underscore, or brackets: LIKE '%[_]%' ESCAPE '\' — _ and % are wildcards, so a bare LIKE '%_%' matches everything
LIKE '%_%' matches only literal underscores
Underscores don't need escaping in LIKE
Use = instead of LIKE for patterns
evidence: SELECT * FROM skus WHERE sku LIKE '%_%'; -- matches every row
scenarios.hint: In LIKE, what do % and _ mean — and how do you search for a literal _?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the pattern match everything, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: Searching SKUs containing a literal underscore returns every row in the table.
scenarios.title: The wildcard that wasn't
scenarios.why: In LIKE, % = any sequence and _ = any single character — so '%_%' means 'anything, then anything, then anything' = all rows. Escape the literal: LIKE '%\_%' ESCAPE '\' (T-SQL also supports bracket syntax: LIKE '%[_]%'). Know your wildcards before pattern-matching.

choices: EXISTS with a correlated subquery — stops at first match, NULL-safe, and expresses 'has at least one' directly
IN with a subquery — identical in all cases
A JOIN with DISTINCT — cleaner and faster always
COUNT(*) > 0 in a scalar subquery — most readable
evidence:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
scenarios.hint: Which construct short-circuits on the first match and ignores NULLs in the subquery?
scenarios.prompt: Why is EXISTS the idiomatic choice here?
scenarios.situation: A 'customers with at least one order' query. The team debates EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN+DISTINCT.
scenarios.title: The 'has orders' query
scenarios.why: EXISTS is a semi-join: it checks existence and stops at the first match per row — efficient and NULL-safe (IN breaks if the subquery yields NULL). JOIN+DISTINCT materializes duplicates then dedupes — wasteful. Use EXISTS for 'has at least one', NOT EXISTS for 'has none'.

scenarios.title: The vanishing NULLs
scenarios.situation: A report of 'customers without email' returns zero rows, but you know un-emailed customers exist. The filter is WHERE email != 'x'.
evidence: SELECT id FROM customers WHERE email <> ''; -- 0 rows
id=7, email=NULL | id=8, email='' | id=9, email='a@b.c'
scenarios.prompt: How do you correctly find customers with no usable email?
choices: WHERE email IS NULL OR email = '' — NULL never satisfies <>, so test it explicitly
WHERE email <> '' is fine; the data must be wrong
WHERE ISNULL(email,'') <> '' works but hides intent; use COALESCE in the app instead
WHERE email = NULL OR email = ''
scenarios.hint: What does NULL <> '' evaluate to — true, false, or something else?
scenarios.why: The NULL comparison never returns true: NULL <> '' evaluates to UNKNOWN, which WHERE discards. Choice 2 is wrong because the data is fine — the predicate is the bug. Choice 3's ISNULL works but the explicit IS NULL version states the two cases (unknown vs empty) clearly. Choice 4 uses = NULL, which is never true. Correct: test NULL explicitly alongside the empty-string check.

scenarios.title: Duplicate rows in UNION vs UNION ALL
scenarios.situation: Two regional sales feeds are combined with UNION, but finance reports the total row count is lower than the sum of the two feeds.
evidence: SELECT * FROM sales_east UNION SELECT * FROM sales_west;
east=120,000 rows, west=95,000 rows, combined=203,000 rows
scenarios.prompt: What explains the missing 12,000 rows, and what should change?
choices: UNION dedupes identical rows across both feeds — 12,000 rows exist in both; use UNION ALL if cross-region duplicates are legitimate
UNION has a row limit; switch to UNION ALL to raise it
The feeds overlap in time; add a date filter to each side
UNION sorts and drops the last page; add ORDER BY to recover them
scenarios.hint: What does UNION do that UNION ALL does not?
scenarios.why: UNION performs an implicit DISTINCT over the combined set, so rows present in both feeds collapse into one — the 12,000 'missing' rows are exact duplicates across regions. Choice 2 is wrong: UNION has no row limit. Choice 3 misdiagnoses; a date filter doesn't restore deduped rows. Choice 4 invents behavior — UNION never drops pages. If the business expects both feeds' rows counted separately (e.g., each region's sales counted), UNION ALL is correct; if duplicates are data errors, keep UNION and fix the feeds.

choices: The GROUP BY grain is wrong — grouping by order_id, product_id counts line items, not orders; group by the order grain (or COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)) for 'orders per customer'
COUNT is broken for large tables
Use SUM instead of COUNT
Add more columns to GROUP BY until the numbers look right
evidence:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM order_lines GROUP BY customer_id; -- inflated vs known order counts
scenarios.hint: What is one row of the grouped input — an order, or an order line?
scenarios.situation: 'Orders per customer' counts are 3x the known order totals. The query groups order_lines by customer_id.
scenarios.title: The inflated counts
scenarios.why: Aggregation grain must match the question's grain: order_lines has one row per line item, so COUNT(*) counts lines, not orders. Fix: COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), or aggregate orders (one row per order) instead. The #1 aggregation bug is grouping at the wrong grain — always ask 'what is one row here?' before trusting a COUNT.

choices: HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before — put the aggregate predicate in HAVING and keep row filters in WHERE
WHERE can filter on COUNT(*) in SQL Server
Move the aggregate to the SELECT list and filter in the app
HAVING and WHERE are interchangeable
evidence:
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales
GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 100000;
scenarios.hint: Can WHERE see the result of SUM? When does SUM even get computed?
scenarios.prompt: Why must the aggregate filter be in HAVING?
scenarios.situation: A 'regions over $100k' query. A junior dev tries WHERE SUM(amount) > 100000 and gets an error.
scenarios.title: The HAVING rule
scenarios.why: WHERE filters input rows before grouping — aggregates don't exist yet. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY computes them. Pattern: WHERE for row predicates (sargable, indexed), GROUP BY, then HAVING for group predicates. (T-SQL also lets you filter on SELECT aliases via subquery/CTE, but HAVING is the direct tool.)

choices: AVG ignores NULL ratings — the average is over raters only; decide whether 'no rating' should count as 0 (then use AVG(COALESCE(rating,0))) or be excluded
AVG includes NULLs as zeros
The query is wrong; averages can't use NULLs at all
Use SUM/COUNT(*) instead — it handles NULLs
evidence: SELECT product_id, AVG(rating) FROM reviews GROUP BY product_id; -- products with few ratings rank high
scenarios.hint: AVG of (5, NULL, NULL) — is it 5, or 1.67?
scenarios.prompt: What does AVG actually compute here, and what decision does it force?
scenarios.situation: Products with one 5-star review outrank products with hundreds of 4.8 averages. AVG(rating) ignores NULL (unrated) rows.
scenarios.title: The misleading average
scenarios.why: All aggregates except COUNT(*) skip NULLs: AVG(5, NULL, NULL) = 5, not 1.67. That's correct for 'average of ratings given' but misleading for ranking — it's a product decision: exclude non-raters (current), count them as 0 (COALESCE), or require a minimum rating count (HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10). The SQL is right; the metric definition needs intent.

choices: GROUPING SETS (or ROLLUP/CUBE) — one pass computing subtotals at multiple grains; GROUPING() distinguishes a real NULL from a subtotal row
Run 4 separate GROUP BY queries and UNION ALL them
GROUP BY with multiple columns gives subtotals automatically
Subtotals require a reporting tool, not SQL
evidence:
SELECT region, quarter, SUM(amount) FROM sales
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region, quarter), (region), ());
scenarios.hint: Which clause computes several GROUP BYs in one scan?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get detail + subtotals + grand total in one query?
scenarios.situation: A report needs sales by (region, quarter), by region subtotal, and a grand total. The team writes three queries and merges in the app.
scenarios.title: The subtotal report
scenarios.why: GROUPING SETS lists multiple groupings computed in one pass: ((region,quarter),(region),()) gives detail rows, region subtotals, and the grand total. ROLLUP(region, quarter) gives the hierarchical chain; CUBE gives all combinations. GROUPING(col) tells subtotal NULLs apart from real NULLs. One scan, one result set — do it in SQL.

choices: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) — counts each customer once; COUNT(*) counts rows (visits)
COUNT(*) — it counts customers
COUNT(customer_id) — same as DISTINCT
SUM(1) with GROUP BY
scenarios.hint: If one customer visited 5 times, how many times should they be counted?
scenarios.prompt: Which count answers 'how many unique customers'?
scenarios.situation: 'Unique visitors per day' is computed with COUNT(*) on a visits table — power users visiting 20x inflate it.
scenarios.title: The unique visitor
scenarios.why: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-NULL values. 'Unique customers' = COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). (COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULLs — usually what you want for 'unique'.)

choices: Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN status='shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) — pivots rows into columns in one pass
A separate query per status, joined together
PIVOT is the only way; CASE can't aggregate
Conditional aggregation requires dynamic SQL
evidence:
SELECT warehouse,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status='pending' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending
FROM orders GROUP BY warehouse;
scenarios.hint: How do you count only the rows matching a condition, inside an aggregate?
scenarios.prompt: What is this pattern called, and why is it better than multiple queries?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard needs shipped/pending/cancelled counts per warehouse. The team runs three queries.
scenarios.title: The pivot in one pass
scenarios.why: Conditional aggregation puts CASE inside the aggregate — one scan produces all three columns. It's portable (works everywhere, unlike PIVOT syntax which varies), composable with any aggregate (SUM/AVG/COUNT), and avoids N queries. The CASE returns 1/0 or NULL (NULLs are ignored by the aggregate) per row.

scenarios.title: HAVING vs WHERE: the misplaced filter
scenarios.situation: A query computing average order value per region for 'regions with 100+ orders' fails: the aggregate condition was placed in WHERE and SQL Server rejects it.
evidence: SELECT region, AVG(total) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 100 GROUP BY region;
An aggregate may not appear in the WHERE clause
choices: Move the aggregate predicate to HAVING: GROUP BY region HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
Wrap the query and filter on the alias in an outer WHERE
Use a subquery in WHERE comparing against a scalar aggregate
Change COUNT(*) to SUM(1) so it is allowed in WHERE
scenarios.hint: At which pipeline stage do aggregates come into existence?
scenarios.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so aggregates don't exist yet at WHERE time — the engine is right to reject it. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, which is exactly 'regions with 100+ orders'. Choice 2 works but is needlessly convoluted. Choice 3 is wrong-shaped for a per-group condition. Choice 4 is nonsense: SUM(1) is equally an aggregate. Correct: HAVING COUNT(*) > 100.

scenarios.title: Counting paid vs refunded in one pass
scenarios.situation: A dashboard needs per-day counts of paid, refunded, and disputed orders. The current code runs three separate queries.
evidence: SELECT day, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY day; -- x3, one per status
orders: 40M rows; three full scans per refresh
choices: One GROUP BY with conditional counts: COUNT(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 END) per status
UNION ALL the three queries — the optimizer merges them
Add an index on (day, status) and keep three queries
PIVOT with dynamic SQL for each status
scenarios.hint: Can one GROUP BY produce three different counts?
scenarios.why: Conditional aggregation computes all three metrics in a single scan and single GROUP BY: COUNT(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN 1 END) counts only matching rows (non-matches yield NULL, ignored by COUNT). Choice 2 still scans three times. Choice 3's index helps each query but triples work remains. Choice 4 adds dynamic-SQL complexity for zero benefit over CASE. Correct: one pass with conditional aggregates.

choices: Predicate placement: putting o.status='shipped' in WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN (NULL-extended rows are filtered out); move it to the ON clause to keep all customers
LEFT JOIN is broken in SQL Server
Use INNER JOIN — LEFT JOIN can't filter
Add ISNULL to the WHERE clause
evidence:
SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'; -- customers without orders vanish
scenarios.hint: What does o.status look like for a customer with no orders — and does it pass the WHERE?
scenarios.prompt: Why do customers without orders disappear?
scenarios.situation: A 'all customers with their shipped orders' report drops customers who have no orders at all.
scenarios.title: The LEFT JOIN that wasn't
scenarios.why: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows, extending missing matches with NULLs — but WHERE o.status='shipped' then rejects those NULL rows (UNKNOWN ≠ TRUE), silently converting the outer join to an inner join. Fix: put the condition in ON (filters the right side before joining, preserving left rows). Rule: conditions on the nullable side belong in ON for outer joins.

choices: Fanout: joining at different grains multiplies rows — one customer × 3 orders × 2 addresses = 6 rows; SUM(amount) double-counts. Pre-aggregate each side to the join grain first
The JOIN syntax is wrong
Use INNER JOIN to reduce rows
Fanout only happens with FULL JOIN
evidence:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
JOIN addresses a ON a.customer_id=c.id
GROUP BY c.name; -- totals 2x actual
scenarios.hint: If a customer has 3 orders and 2 addresses, how many joined rows — and what does SUM see?
scenarios.situation: Revenue per customer is 2x actual after joining orders and addresses. Each join is individually correct.
scenarios.title: The fanout trap
scenarios.why: Joining two one-to-many relationships at different grains multiplies rows (3 orders × 2 addresses = 6 rows per customer), and SUM then counts each order twice. Fix: aggregate each side to the common grain (customer) before joining, or aggregate in subqueries/CTEs. Whenever totals look multiplied, check join fanout first.

choices: NOT EXISTS (correlated anti-join) — NULL-safe and stops at first match; NOT IN fails if the subquery returns any NULL
NOT IN — simplest and always correct
LEFT JOIN with IS NULL — the only NULL-safe option
EXCEPT — identical to NOT IN
evidence:
SELECT * FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS
 (SELECT 1 FROM order_lines ol WHERE ol.product_id = p.product_id);
scenarios.hint: What does NOT IN do when the subquery contains a NULL?
scenarios.prompt: Which anti-join pattern is robust, and why not NOT IN?
scenarios.situation: 'Products never ordered' — the team debates NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS vs LEFT JOIN/IS NULL.
scenarios.title: The never-ordered products
scenarios.why: NOT IN (subquery with NULL) → every comparison is UNKNOWN → zero rows. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe (correlated predicate per row) and short-circuits. LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL is equivalent and sometimes clearer. Rule: for anti-joins, NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN/IS NULL; treat NOT IN as guilty until proven NULL-free.

choices: Self join with aliases: FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id — the table plays two roles
Subqueries can't reference the same table twice
UNION the table with itself
Self joins require temp tables
evidence:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
scenarios.hint: How do you put the same table on both sides of a join?
scenarios.prompt: What pattern resolves a hierarchy stored in one table?
scenarios.situation: Employees table has manager_id → id. Report needs employee + manager name. LEFT JOIN keeps the CEO (no manager).
scenarios.title: The org chart query
scenarios.why: A self join aliases the table twice (e, m) so it plays both roles: employee row and manager row. LEFT JOIN preserves top-level rows with no manager (NULL manager name). For multi-level hierarchies, recursive CTEs walk the chain.

choices: FULL OUTER JOIN — keeps unmatched rows from both sides; unmatched columns are NULL on the missing side
UNION of two LEFT JOINs — the only way
FULL JOIN is the same as CROSS JOIN
INNER JOIN with COALESCE
scenarios.hint: Which join keeps the orphans from BOTH tables?
scenarios.prompt: When is FULL OUTER JOIN the right tool?
scenarios.situation: Reconciling two systems' customer lists: find customers in A only, B only, and both.
scenarios.title: The reconciliation
scenarios.why: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched pairs plus unmatched rows from both sides (NULLs where the other side is missing) — the reconciliation shape in one query. Filter WHERE a.id IS NULL (B-only) or b.id IS NULL (A-only) for the exceptions. INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps only one side's orphans.

choices: Join order rarely matters to the optimizer (it reorders), but predicate placement and join type do — write for clarity; check the actual plan for the real order
Always join the smallest table first — the optimizer can't reorder
Join order determines the result
Use parentheses to force order always
scenarios.hint: Does the modern optimizer execute joins in the order you wrote them?
scenarios.situation: A developer carefully orders joins 'smallest first' for performance, and the plan shows a different order.
scenarios.title: The join-order myth
scenarios.why: Cost-based optimizers reorder joins freely — written order is about readability, not execution. What matters: correct join types, sargable predicates, accurate statistics. (Hints/parentheses can force order, but that's an override for diagnosed cases, not a default.) Write joins in the order humans follow best; let the optimizer do its job.

scenarios.title: The missing customers
scenarios.situation: A 'customers with their open orders' report uses LEFT JOIN but customers without orders are absent. The query filters o.status = 'open' in WHERE.
evidence: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.status='open';
customers with no orders missing from output
choices: Move the predicate into ON: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='open'
Change to INNER JOIN — the WHERE already implies it
Add OR o.status IS NULL to the WHERE clause
Use a subquery filtering orders first, then LEFT JOIN it
scenarios.hint: For a customer with no orders, what is o.status after the join?
scenarios.why: WHERE filters the joined result: for customers with no orders, o.status is NULL, and NULL='open' is UNKNOWN — the row is discarded, silently converting the LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN. Moving the predicate to ON applies it during matching, so unmatched customers survive with NULLs. Choice 2 accepts the bug as intended behavior — wrong requirement. Choice 3 works but is fragile and obscures intent. Choice 4 also works (filtered derived table) but the ON-clause fix is the idiomatic one-liner. Correct: predicate in ON.

scenarios.title: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS with NULLs
scenarios.situation: An anti-join 'customers with no orders' using NOT IN returns zero rows, though most customers never ordered. orders.customer_id is nullable.
evidence: SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
choices: Rewrite with NOT EXISTS: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
Add WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL inside the NOT IN subquery
Use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL instead
NOT IN is fine; rebuild the index on orders.customer_id
scenarios.hint: What does `5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` evaluate to?
scenarios.why: One NULL in the NOT IN list poisons every comparison: id <> NULL is UNKNOWN for all rows, so WHERE keeps nothing. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe by construction (correlated equality with NULL never matches, which is the desired semantics). Choice 2 also fixes it and is legitimate, but NOT EXISTS is the idiomatic, optimizer-friendly standard. Choice 3 is equally correct but more verbose. Choice 4 is irrelevant — indexes don't change three-valued logic. Correct: NOT EXISTS.

choices: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1 — partitioned ranking picks the top row per group; GROUP BY can't return the whole row
GROUP BY dept with MAX(salary) — then join back (works but two passes)
TOP 1 overall — gives one row total
RANK() without PARTITION BY
scenarios.hint: Which function numbers rows within each partition, so rn=1 is the top of each group?
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic top-N-per-group pattern?
scenarios.situation: 'Highest-paid employee per department, with full row details.' GROUP BY loses the row details.
scenarios.title: The top per group
scenarios.why: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows within each department; the outer filter rn=1 keeps each department's top earner with all columns. GROUP BY + MAX needs a self-join to recover the row. RANK()/DENSE_RANK() differ on ties: ROW_NUMBER is arbitrary among ties, RANK skips numbers, DENSE_RANK doesn't.

choices: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — explicit running frame; the default frame (RANGE) misbehaves with duplicate ORDER BY values
SUM without OVER — it aggregates everything
The default frame is always ROWS
Running totals need a self join
scenarios.hint: With duplicate dates, does RANGE treat tied rows as one peer group or separate rows?
scenarios.situation: A running total looks right until duplicate dates appear — then tied days get the same cumulative value (peer-group behavior).
scenarios.title: The running total
scenarios.why: The default window frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — RANGE treats tied ORDER BY values as peers, giving them identical results. ROWS counts physical rows, so each row accumulates independently. For running totals, be explicit: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Know your frame: ROWS = physical, RANGE = logical peers.

choices: LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY product ORDER BY day) — previous row's value per product; then compute the difference
A self join on day-1 — simpler and faster
LEAD looks backward
LAG can't partition
scenarios.hint: Which function reaches one row back within the partition?
scenarios.prompt: How do you compare each row to its predecessor?
scenarios.situation: Day-over-day sales change per product. The team considers a self-join on date arithmetic.
scenarios.title: The day-over-day delta
scenarios.why: LAG(expr) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY day) returns the previous row's value within each product's timeline — no self-join, no date arithmetic, handles gaps naturally. LEAD looks forward. The PARTITION BY restarts the sequence per product; without it, products would bleed into each other.

choices: ROW_NUMBER: unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily; RANK: ties share a rank, next rank skips; DENSE_RANK: ties share, no skipping — pick by whether ties should share and whether numbering must be gapless
They are identical; names are historical
RANK never has ties
DENSE_RANK always skips numbers
scenarios.hint: Two players tie at 100 — what rank does the 90 get under each function?
scenarios.prompt: How do the three ranking functions differ on ties?
scenarios.situation: A leaderboard must handle tied scores. The product spec says 'tied players share a rank, and the next rank continues sequentially'.
scenarios.title: The tied leaderboard
scenarios.why: ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3 — unique, arbitrary among ties. RANK: 1,1,3 — ties share, numbering skips (competition ranking). DENSE_RANK: 1,1,2 — ties share, no gaps. The spec ('share rank, sequential next') = DENSE_RANK. Choosing wrong silently misranks — match the function to the spec.

choices: Aggregate OVER () without GROUP BY — SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER () FROM employees keeps every row with the global average attached
GROUP BY with the average joined back
Window functions require GROUP BY
Subquery in SELECT for the average
scenarios.hint: Which OVER() form computes an aggregate over the whole result without collapsing rows?
scenarios.prompt: How do you attach an aggregate to every row without collapsing?
scenarios.situation: 'Each employee with their salary vs the company average.' GROUP BY would collapse the rows.
scenarios.title: The average on every row
scenarios.why: An aggregate with OVER() (empty = whole result set, or PARTITION BY for per-group) computes without collapsing rows — each row keeps its detail plus the aggregate. That's the window function superpower: aggregates at any grain alongside detail rows. GROUP BY is for collapsing; OVER() is for annotating.

choices: FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE with explicit frame — LAST_VALUE needs ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or it returns the current row (default frame ends at current row)
LAST_VALUE works with the default frame
FIRST_VALUE needs a frame too
Use MIN/MAX instead — identical semantics
scenarios.hint: The default frame ends at the current row — what does LAST_VALUE see then?
scenarios.prompt: Why does LAST_VALUE need an explicit frame?
scenarios.situation: FIRST_VALUE works; LAST_VALUE returns the current row's value instead of the partition's last value.
scenarios.title: The LAST_VALUE surprise
scenarios.why: Default frame = RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, so LAST_VALUE's 'last' is the current row — usually not what's wanted. Extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for the true partition end. FIRST_VALUE is unaffected (partition start is always in frame). Another frame-semantics trap: always state the frame when using FIRST/LAST_VALUE.

scenarios.title: RANK ties and the off-by-one podium
scenarios.situation: A 'top 3 sales reps' leaderboard uses RANK() and sometimes shows 4 or 5 people. Management wants exactly 3 names.
evidence: SELECT rep, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC) AS r FROM reps; -- outer filter r <= 3
ties at rank 3 pull extra reps onto the podium
scenarios.prompt: How do you guarantee exactly 3 names?
choices: Use ROW_NUMBER() instead of RANK() so ties get distinct numbers, with a deterministic tie-breaker in ORDER BY
Keep RANK() and filter r < 3
Use DENSE_RANK() — it never produces gaps
Add DISTINCT to the outer query
scenarios.hint: Which function guarantees unique numbers even with ties?
scenarios.why: RANK() assigns tied rows the same rank, so r <= 3 can match 5 rows when 3 reps tie for 3rd. ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a unique number — exactly 3 rows satisfy rn <= 3. The ORDER BY must be deterministic (add rep id as tie-breaker) or which tied rep survives is arbitrary. Choice 2 just moves the boundary problem to rank 2. Choice 3 is wrong: DENSE_RANK also shares ranks across ties. Choice 4 does nothing — rows are already distinct. Correct: ROW_NUMBER with deterministic ordering.

scenarios.title: Frame boundaries: ROWS vs RANGE
scenarios.situation: A 7-day moving average sometimes averages 9 or 10 rows. The frame is RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW over ORDER BY day.
evidence: AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
day has duplicate dates (multiple batches per day)
choices: Change RANGE to ROWS so the frame is exactly 7 physical rows regardless of duplicate dates
Deduplicate the dates first with DISTINCT
Change 6 PRECEDING to 7 PRECEDING
Use LAG(revenue, 6) instead of the frame
scenarios.hint: Is RANGE counting rows, or counting distinct date values?
scenarios.why: RANGE is value-based: 6 PRECEDING means 'rows whose day is within 6 days', and all peers sharing a boundary date are included — with duplicate dates the frame holds more than 7 rows. ROWS is physical: exactly the 6 rows above plus current = 7 rows always. Choice 2 destroys the per-batch granularity the business may need. Choice 3 misdiagnoses the mechanism. Choice 4 computes a single lagged value, not an average. Correct: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.

choices: TRY/CATCH with explicit transaction control: BEGIN TRY/BEGIN TRAN ... COMMIT; BEGIN CATCH ... IF @@TRANCOUNT>0 ROLLBACK; THROW; — THROW preserves the original error
@@ERROR checks after every statement — sufficient and modern
TRY/CATCH without transaction handling — partial commits are fine
RAISERROR without rollback — the transaction auto-rolls-back
scenarios.hint: If the second UPDATE fails, what happens to the first without a ROLLBACK?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct error-handling pattern for a multi-statement transaction?
scenarios.situation: A funds-transfer procedure must debit and credit atomically. On failure, nothing may persist, and the caller must see the real error.
scenarios.title: The transfer procedure
scenarios.why: TRY/CATCH + explicit transaction: on error, CATCH rolls back the open transaction (@@TRANCOUNT check) and THROW re-raises the original error with its number/line — the caller gets truth, not a masked message. RAISERROR with a custom message loses the original context unless carefully preserved. Never leave a transaction half-committed.

choices: CTE for readability of a single use; temp table (#t) for reuse across statements, indexing, or large sets; table variable (@t) for small sets — but it has no statistics, so the optimizer guesses 1 row
Table variables are always fastest
Temp tables can't be indexed
CTEs are materialized and reusable
scenarios.hint: Which one can be indexed and referenced twice, and which one makes the optimizer assume 1 row?
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose between CTE, temp table, and table variable?
scenarios.situation: A procedure stages 2M rows, filters them twice, and joins the result. A table variable makes it crawl.
scenarios.title: The staging choice
scenarios.why: CTE: a named subquery — readable, single-use, not materialized (re-evaluated per reference). #temp table: real tempdb table — indexable, statistics, reusable across statements — right for large/multi-use staging. @table variable: no statistics (optimizer assumes 1 row pre-2019 / fixed guesses), no parallel plans historically — fine for small sets, poison for 2M rows. Match the tool to size and reuse.

choices: sp_executesql with parameters — parameterized, plan-reusable, injection-safe; EXEC(string) concatenates and is injectable
String concatenation with EXEC — simplest and safe if you trust the input
Dynamic SQL is never needed
sp_executesql can't take parameters
evidence:
DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = @s';
EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N'@s VARCHAR(20)', @s = @status;
scenarios.hint: Which one keeps user input as data, never as code?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe dynamic-SQL pattern?
scenarios.situation: A search procedure builds WHERE clauses dynamically from optional filters. The first version concatenates user input.
scenarios.title: The dynamic search
scenarios.why: sp_executesql with declared parameters keeps input as data — parameterized, injection-proof, with reusable plans. EXEC(@string) with concatenation lets input become code (classic injection). Dynamic SQL is legitimate for optional-filter searches; just parameterize it. Never concatenate user input into SQL text.

choices: SET NOCOUNT ON — suppresses '(n rows affected)' messages that confuse clients/ORMs; SET XACT_ABORT ON — auto-rolls-back on runtime errors
They are obsolete; defaults are fine
NOCOUNT breaks result sets
XACT_ABORT commits on error
scenarios.hint: Which setting turns DONE_IN_PROC messages off, and which makes errors abort the transaction?
scenarios.prompt: What do these two SET options do, and why are they procedure boilerplate?
scenarios.situation: A procedure's row-count messages break an ORM's result mapping; a mid-procedure error leaves a partial transaction.
scenarios.title: The procedure boilerplate
scenarios.why: SET NOCOUNT ON stops the '(1 row affected)' messages that pollute result streams and confuse drivers. SET XACT_ABORT ON makes most runtime errors abort the batch and roll back the transaction — fail-atomic instead of fail-partial. Both are standard procedure headers for predictable behavior.

choices: OUTPUT clause — INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... OUTPUT inserted.id captures affected rows in one statement, no second query, no race
SELECT after the DML — simple and race-free
@@IDENTITY after insert — safest scope
Triggers to capture IDs
evidence:
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total)
OUTPUT inserted.order_id VALUES (5, 99.00);
scenarios.hint: Which clause returns the new identity values from the same statement that created them?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get the new IDs back atomically?
scenarios.situation: After inserting orders, the app needs the generated order_ids. SELECT MAX(id) races under concurrency.
scenarios.title: The new identity
scenarios.why: OUTPUT inserted.<cols> returns affected rows from the DML statement itself — atomic, no race, no extra round trip. SELECT MAX(id) is broken under concurrency. (SCOPE_IDENTITY() is the scalar alternative for single-row inserts; @@IDENTITY is trigger-polluted — avoid.)

choices: Stored procedure for actions/workflows (can have side effects, no return-value requirement); function for computations (deterministic-ish, usable in queries, no side effects like DML on base tables)
Functions can do anything procedures can
Procedures can't return values
Use functions for ETL workflows
scenarios.hint: Which one can you call from inside a SELECT, and which one is barred from side effects there?
scenarios.prompt: When do you write a procedure vs a function?
scenarios.situation: A 'calculate discount' logic is needed both in SELECT queries and in an ETL step that logs to an audit table.
scenarios.title: The procedure/function split
scenarios.why: Functions: callable inline in queries, must be side-effect-free (no DML on base tables, deterministic preferred) — perfect for 'calculate discount'. Procedures: invoked with EXEC, can do anything (DML, transactions, multiple result sets) — right for workflows like the ETL step with audit logging. Scalar UDFs in big queries can hurt performance (row-by-row); inline table-valued functions are the performant function shape.

scenarios.title: OUTPUT vs SCOPE_IDENTITY in T-SQL
scenarios.situation: An order-entry procedure inserts a header then line items. Under load, line items occasionally attach to the wrong order. It uses @@IDENTITY to get the new order id.
evidence: INSERT INTO orders ...; SET @oid = @@IDENTITY; INSERT INTO line_items ... @oid ...
orders has an AFTER INSERT trigger writing to audit_log (which has its own identity)
choices: Use SCOPE_IDENTITY() (or the OUTPUT clause), which is unaffected by the trigger's identity insert
Use IDENT_CURRENT('orders') — it reads the table directly
Add WITH (NOLOCK) to the line_items insert
Wrap both inserts in a transaction
scenarios.hint: Whose identity did the trigger generate — and in which scope?
scenarios.why: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity generated in the session — including the trigger's audit_log insert, so @oid sometimes holds an audit id, not the order id. SCOPE_IDENTITY() returns the last identity in the current scope only (the orders insert). The OUTPUT clause (OUTPUT inserted.id) is equally correct and works for multi-row inserts. Choice 2 is worse: IDENT_CURRENT is session-independent and races under concurrency. Choice 3 is nonsense for correctness. Choice 4 doesn't fix which id was captured. Correct: SCOPE_IDENTITY() or OUTPUT.

scenarios.title: TRY/CATCH with a doomed transaction
scenarios.situation: A procedure's CATCH block rolls back and re-throws, but callers report 'transaction count mismatch' errors after certain failures.
evidence: BEGIN TRY BEGIN TRAN; ...; COMMIT; END TRY BEGIN CATCH ROLLBACK; THROW; END CATCH
some errors leave @@TRANCOUNT inconsistent for the caller
choices: Check XACT_STATE() in CATCH: if -1 (doomed) roll back; only commit when XACT_STATE()=1; guard ROLLBACK with IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
Remove TRY/CATCH and let errors bubble naturally
Add SET XACT_ABORT OFF so transactions survive errors
Commit in the CATCH block to balance the count
scenarios.hint: Can every failed transaction still be committed?
scenarios.why: Severe errors doom the transaction (XACT_STATE() = -1): it can only roll back, and a bare ROLLBACK without checking @@TRANCOUNT can itself error when the transaction already aborted, unbalancing the caller's count. The robust pattern: CATCH checks XACT_STATE — -1 means uncommittable (roll back), 1 means committable. Choice 2 abandons structured handling. Choice 3 is backwards: XACT_ABORT ON is the safe default for write procedures. Choice 4 commits partial work — a correctness disaster. Correct: XACT_STATE-guarded handling.

choices: Sargable predicates — WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' lets the index seek; wrapping the column in a function (YEAR(created_at)=2026) forces a scan of every row
Functions on columns help the optimizer
Indexes work the same with functions on columns
Scans are always faster than seeks
evidence:
-- slow: WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026
-- fast: WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'
scenarios.hint: Can the index seek when the indexed value is hidden inside a function call?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the function-wrapped predicate slow?
scenarios.situation: A date-range query takes minutes. The predicate is WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026 on an indexed column.
scenarios.title: The unsargable predicate
scenarios.why: Sargable = Search ARGument ABLE: the optimizer can seek the index when the column appears bare in a range/equality predicate. Wrapping it in YEAR() hides the value — every row must be computed and compared (scan). Rewrite as a range on the bare column. Same for UPPER(name)='X' (use a case-insensitive collation or computed persisted column) and CAST on indexed columns.

choices: The actual execution plan — read operator costs, seek vs scan, and the estimated-vs-actual row counts; a huge gap means stale statistics
Add the index the missing-index hint suggests — hints are always right
Estimated plan is enough; actuals don't matter
Rebuild all indexes weekly as routine
scenarios.hint: Estimated 100 rows, actual 2M — what does that gap diagnose?
scenarios.prompt: How do you read a plan for the root cause?
scenarios.situation: A query suddenly slows. The actual plan shows a nested loop over an estimated 100 rows but 2M actual rows.
scenarios.title: The plan that lied
scenarios.why: Estimated vs actual row counts: a big gap = the optimizer decided on bad cardinality — usually stale/missing statistics (UPDATE STATISTICS) or skewed data needing filtered stats. The plan names the operators (seek vs scan, loop vs hash vs merge join); the row-count gap names the cause. Missing-index hints are suggestions, not prescriptions — validate before creating.

choices: Parameter sniffing — the plan was compiled for an atypical first parameter value and cached; options: OPTIMIZE FOR, recompile hints, or plan guides after diagnosis
Parameter sniffing is a myth
Always use RECOMPILE everywhere — no downside
The solution is always more indexes
scenarios.hint: The query is fast for some parameter values and slow for others, with the same plan. What was the plan built for?
scenarios.prompt: What is parameter sniffing, and what are the principled responses?
scenarios.situation: A procedure is fast for common customer IDs, glacial for rare ones — same cached plan. Recompiling fixes it temporarily.
scenarios.title: The sometimes-slow procedure
scenarios.why: On first execution, SQL Server 'sniffs' the parameter values and compiles a plan optimal for them, then reuses it for all values. Skewed data → one plan can't fit all. Responses (after diagnosis): OPTIMIZE FOR (@p = typical / UNKNOWN), OPTION (RECOMPILE) for wildly varying values (CPU cost per compile), or plan guides. Don't carpet-bomb RECOMPILE — each compile costs CPU.

choices: N+1: one query for the list + N queries for details — fix with a single JOIN (or batched fetch); watch ORM lazy-loading
N+1 is fine; databases are fast
Add caching instead of fixing the queries
N+1 only happens with cursors
scenarios.hint: If the page loads 50 orders, how many queries run — 1, or 51?
scenarios.prompt: What is the N+1 problem, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: An order page runs 1 query for 50 orders, then 50 queries for line items. Page load: 8 seconds.
scenarios.title: The chatty page
scenarios.why: N+1: 1 query gets N parents, then N queries fetch children — 51 round trips, usually from ORM lazy loading. Fix: one JOIN (or two batched queries: parents, then children WHERE parent_id IN (...)) — set-based retrieval. It's the most common app-layer SQL performance bug; the database isn't slow, the chatter is.

choices: Covering index on (customer_id, order_date) INCLUDE (total) — seeks the predicate and covers the output, no key lookups; but every index taxes writes
Index every column separately — more indexes, more speed
INCLUDE columns are searchable in seeks
A clustered index on total
scenarios.hint: Which index serves the WHERE and the SELECT without touching the table?
scenarios.prompt: What index design serves this query fully?
scenarios.situation: SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id=@c AND order_date > @d does key lookups for every row — the nonclustered index lacks total.
scenarios.title: The lookup-heavy query
scenarios.why: A covering index includes all columns the query needs: key columns (customer_id, order_date) support the seek; INCLUDE (total) carries the payload without widening the key. No key lookups → pure index seek. Cost: wider index, slower writes, more maintenance. INCLUDE columns aren't seekable — they're payload. Design indexes per query pattern, not per column.

choices: Set-based single statement — one UPDATE with a join/set operation; cursors process row-by-row with per-row overhead
Cursors are faster for large sets
WHILE loops with temp tables beat set operations
Set-based only works for SELECTs
evidence:
-- slow: CURSOR over 500k rows, one UPDATE per fetch
-- fast: UPDATE t SET x = s.x FROM target t JOIN staging s ON s.id = t.id;
scenarios.hint: How many round trips through the engine: 500k, or 1?
scenarios.prompt: Why is the cursor version slow, and what replaces it?
scenarios.situation: A 500k-row sync uses a cursor with per-row UPDATEs. It runs for 40 minutes.
scenarios.title: The 40-minute cursor
scenarios.why: Cursors/WHILE loops pay per-row overhead (fetch, context, logging per statement) — 500k iterations of overhead. A single set-based UPDATE...FROM processes all rows in one plan, one pass. Databases are built for sets; row-by-row is fighting the engine. (Cursors have rare legitimate uses — ordered procedural logic — but bulk data movement isn't one.)

scenarios.title: The implicit conversion that killed the seek
scenarios.situation: An orders lookup by customer_id slowed 100x after an app change. The plan shows an index scan with a CONVERT_IMPLICIT warning on customer_id.
evidence: CONVERT_IMPLICIT(int, orders.customer_id, 0) — index scan, 40M rows read
app started sending customer_id as INT; column is VARCHAR(20)
choices: Send the parameter as VARCHAR(20) matching the column type (or convert the parameter, never the column)
Rebuild the index on customer_id
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) to the query
Change the column to INT
scenarios.hint: Which side of the comparison got wrapped in CONVERT — and which side should be converted instead?
scenarios.why: When types mismatch, SQL Server converts the column (higher precedence wins), wrapping it in CONVERT_IMPLICIT — the predicate is no longer sargable, so the seek becomes a 40M-row scan. Converting the parameter side instead keeps the column bare and the seek intact. Choice 2 can't fix a conversion. Choice 3 addresses sniffing, not conversions. Choice 4 (alter the column) is a bigger migration — valid long-term, but the immediate correct fix is matching the parameter type. Correct: type-match the parameter.

scenarios.title: Parameter sniffing: fast for one value, slow for another
scenarios.situation: A reporting procedure runs in 2s for common @region values but 90s for one rare region. Same query, same plan shape, wildly different row counts.
evidence: plan compiled for @region='West' (2M rows, hash join) reused for @region='FarNorth' (200 rows)
statistics are current; estimated vs actual rows match the sniffed value
scenarios.prompt: What is the best first step?
choices: Test OPTION (RECOMPILE): if per-execution compilation fixes it, the plan was the problem — then decide between recompile, OPTIMIZE FOR, or separate code paths
Update statistics with FULLSCAN
Add a covering index on region
Increase the procedure's timeout
scenarios.hint: What parameter value was the cached plan compiled for?
scenarios.why: The plan was compiled and cached for the first-seen parameter value; the rare region reuses a hash-join plan built for 2M rows. OPTION (RECOMPILE) compiles per execution — if the rare region drops to 2s, sniffing is confirmed, and you then choose the durable fix (recompile for a rarely-run report, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, or branch logic). Choice 2 is wrong: stats are current and estimates match the sniffed value. Choice 3 may help generally but doesn't address plan choice. Choice 4 masks the symptom. Correct: confirm with RECOMPILE, then pick the structural fix.

scenarios.title: The Queries Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Queries is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Queries?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Queries issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Queries is too complex to troubleshoot systematically

This method works for any Queries failure in Sql.

evidence: All Queries components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
