domains.name: Indexing & Execution Plans
domains.description: B-tree indexes, composite column order, covering indexes, sargability, and maintenance.

scenarios.title: Composite index, wrong column order
scenarios.situation: A query filters WHERE customer_id=@c AND order_date BETWEEN @a AND @b. The index is (order_date, customer_id) and the plan still scans.
evidence: CREATE INDEX ix ON orders(order_date, customer_id);
WHERE customer_id = @c AND order_date BETWEEN @a AND @b
index scan over the full date range, residual predicate on customer_id
scenarios.prompt: What index design serves this query?
choices: (customer_id, order_date): equality first seeks to the customer's slice, then the date range narrows within it
Keep (order_date, customer_id) — the optimizer should reorder the predicates
Two single-column indexes; the optimizer will intersect them
A clustered index on order_date
scenarios.hint: Which column's predicate is equality, and which is a range?
scenarios.why: B-tree seeks need the left-most key: with (order_date, customer_id), the engine can only seek the date range (huge), then filter customer_id as a residual. Equality-first (customer_id, order_date) seeks exactly one customer's contiguous range, then applies the date range inside it — orders of magnitude fewer reads. Choice 2 is wrong: predicate order in SQL doesn't change index key order. Choice 3's index intersection is possible but far less efficient than one proper composite. Choice 4 doesn't fix the composite order problem. Correct: (customer_id, order_date).

scenarios.title: Key lookup storm on a hot query
scenarios.situation: A dashboard query runs 50x/sec: seeks an index on orders(customer_id) then does 2M key lookups/sec for total and status.
evidence: SELECT total, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = @c;
choices: Add INCLUDE (total, status): CREATE INDEX ... ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (total, status) — the query is covered, lookups vanish
Widen the key: ON orders(customer_id, total, status)
Make it a clustered index on customer_id
Add OPTION (MAXDOP 8) to parallelize the lookups
scenarios.hint: The seek is fine — what happens after each seek?
scenarios.why: The query needs total and status, which aren't in the index — every row pays a key lookup into the clustered index. INCLUDE puts them in the leaf without widening the key (key width affects tree depth and seek cost). Choice 2 works functionally but bloats keys unnecessarily. Choice 3 reorders the whole table for one query — absurd tradeoff. Choice 4 parallelizes waste instead of removing it. Correct: INCLUDE covering index.

scenarios.title: Filtered index for the hot subset
scenarios.situation: 95% of order queries filter WHERE status='open' (5% of rows), but the index on (status, order_date) is huge and slow to maintain.
evidence: all hot queries: WHERE status='open' AND order_date > @d
CREATE INDEX ix ON orders(status, order_date); — 40M rows indexed
choices: Filtered index: CREATE INDEX ix ON orders(order_date) WHERE status='open' — 2M rows, smaller, faster maintains and seeks
Partition the table by status
Drop the status column from the index key
A columnstore index on the whole table
scenarios.hint: Do the cold 95% of rows need to be in this index at all?
scenarios.why: Every hot query filters status='open', so indexing the other 38M rows is pure write overhead. A filtered index stores only matching rows — smaller, cheaper to maintain, and the optimizer matches queries whose predicate implies the filter. Choice 2 (partitioning) is heavy machinery for a 5% subset. Choice 3 keeps the full-size index. Choice 4 is for analytics scans, not selective seeks. Correct: filtered index.

scenarios.title: Function-wrapped date filter
scenarios.situation: A yearly report WHERE YEAR(order_date)=2026 scans 40M rows despite an index on order_date.
choices: Rewrite as a range: WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2027-01-01' — the column stays bare and the index seeks
Create an index on YEAR(order_date)
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE)
Partition by year
scenarios.hint: Can the engine seek an index when the key column is inside a function?
scenarios.why: YEAR(order_date) wraps the column in a function, so the engine must evaluate it per row — 40M evaluations, no seek possible. The range rewrite expresses identical logic with the column bare, seeking exactly 2026's slice. Choice 2 (indexed computed column) also works but adds schema; the rewrite is free. Choice 3 is irrelevant. Choice 4 is overkill for a predicate bug. Correct: sargable range.

scenarios.title: Fragmentation: measure before rebuilding
scenarios.situation: A nightly job rebuilds all indexes. Maintenance windows are shrinking and the job now overruns into business hours.
evidence: ALTER INDEX ALL ON every_table REBUILD — nightly, 3 hours
choices: Rebuild/reorganize by measured thresholds (e.g., >30% + >1000 pages → rebuild; 5-30% → reorganize); skip the rest
Switch to REORGANIZE for everything — it's always online
Increase FILLFACTOR to 100 on all indexes
Run the rebuilds in parallel with MAXDOP 0
scenarios.hint: What fraction of the rebuilt indexes actually needed it?
scenarios.why: Most of the work is waste: tiny indexes gain nothing from rebuilds, and low-fragmentation indexes don't need them. Threshold-driven maintenance does a fraction of the work with identical benefit. Choice 2 still processes every index nightly. Choice 3 is backwards — FILLFACTOR 100 leaves no room for inserts (more splits); and it's not the problem. Choice 4 speeds up waste. Correct: measure, then act on thresholds.

scenarios.title: GUID clustered keys fragment
scenarios.situation: A table with a NEWID() clustered PK shows 99% fragmentation hours after each rebuild, and inserts are slow.
evidence: id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWID() PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED
heavy random inserts; page splits constant
choices: Change the clustered key to a sequential surrogate (IDENTITY) and make the GUID a nonclustered unique index if still needed
Rebuild more often
Set FILLFACTOR 50 on the clustered index
Switch to NEWSEQUENTIALID() and keep the clustered GUID
scenarios.hint: Where in the B-tree does each new random GUID land?
scenarios.why: Random GUIDs insert into random pages — every insert splits pages, fragmenting the index as fast as it's rebuilt. A sequential IDENTITY clustered key appends to the end (near-zero fragmentation); the GUID becomes a narrow nonclustered unique index. Choice 2 fights physics. Choice 3 halves page density permanently — a costly band-aid. Choice 4 (NEWSEQUENTIALID) genuinely helps and is the minimal change, but sequential IDs are still better understood, narrower, and friendlier to every nonclustered index (which all carry the clustering key). Correct: sequential clustered key.

scenarios.title: Reading the missing-index hint critically
scenarios.situation: The plan suggests a missing index with 95% impact. A junior DBA wants to create every suggested index immediately.
evidence: CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (total) — impact 95%
the suggested INCLUDE list grows with every new query variant
choices: Treat hints as per-query suggestions: consolidate across the workload into a few well-designed indexes instead of creating one per hint
Create it exactly as suggested — 95% impact is 95% impact
Create it, then drop it next week if unused
Ignore all missing-index hints; they're always wrong
scenarios.hint: Is the hint optimizing one query or your whole workload?
scenarios.why: Missing-index hints are narrow: each reflects one query's wish, and blindly creating them yields dozens of overlapping near-duplicate indexes that tax every write. The disciplined move is to aggregate suggestions across the workload and design a few composite/covering indexes serving many queries. Choice 2 creates index sprawl. Choice 3 is churn, not design. Choice 4 throws away a useful signal. Correct: consolidate, then create deliberately.

domains.name: Transactions & Concurrency
domains.description: ACID, isolation levels, locking, deadlocks, and safe concurrent data access.

scenarios.title: Checkout transaction design
scenarios.situation: Checkout does: decrement inventory, create order, charge payment. A crash between steps has left inventory decremented with no order.
evidence: three separate statements, no explicit transaction
crash after step 1 → phantom inventory loss
choices: Wrap all three in one transaction with TRY/CATCH + XACT_ABORT ON; validate preconditions first; keep it short
Run each step in its own transaction for speed
Decrement inventory last so crashes lose nothing
Retry the whole checkout on any failure without a transaction
scenarios.hint: Which of the three steps may commit alone today?
scenarios.why: The three steps are one business atom: wrap in BEGIN/COMMIT so a crash rolls back all of them. TRY/CATCH + XACT_ABORT ON guarantees rollback on error; precondition checks (stock available, payment valid) happen before BEGIN so the transaction stays short. Choice 2 makes partial failure permanent. Choice 3 just moves the hole. Choice 4 without a transaction can double-charge. Correct: single atomic transaction.

scenarios.title: Phantom reads in a balance report
scenarios.situation: A funds-transfer validation reads the balance, checks sufficiency, then debits — under load, accounts go negative. Isolation is READ COMMITTED.
evidence: SELECT @b = balance ...; IF @b >= @amt UPDATE ... SET balance -= @amt;
two concurrent transfers both see 100, both debit 80 → -60
choices: Make the check-and-debit atomic: UPDATE ... SET balance -= @amt WHERE id=@id AND balance >= @amt, then check @@ROWCOUNT
Raise isolation to SERIALIZABLE around the read
Add UPDLOCK to the SELECT
Run the check in a separate transaction
scenarios.hint: Can you express 'debit only if sufficient' as one statement?
scenarios.why: The race is between the read and the write: both sessions read 100 before either writes. The atomic UPDATE folds the check into the write itself — the WHERE clause is evaluated under the write lock, so only one session's predicate can be true. @@ROWCOUNT tells the loser to abort cleanly. Choice 2 works but serializes more than needed. Choice 3 (UPDLOCK) also works but holds locks longer. Choice 4 makes the race worse. Correct: single atomic conditional UPDATE.

scenarios.title: Deadlock from inconsistent access order
scenarios.situation: Two procedures deadlock regularly: ProcA updates accounts then audit_log; ProcB updates audit_log then accounts. Deadlock graphs confirm the cycle.
evidence: T1: accounts(X) waits audit_log; T2: audit_log(X) waits accounts
victims retried, but deadlocks persist at 50/hour
choices: Standardize access order: both procedures touch accounts before audit_log
Increase the deadlock retry count
Set DEADLOCK_PRIORITY HIGH on ProcA
Add NOLOCK hints to the reads
scenarios.hint: Draw the lock-acquisition order of each procedure — where is the cycle?
scenarios.why: The cycle exists because the two procedures acquire the same locks in opposite order. Retries (choice 2) make victims survivable but the 50/hour rate is pure wasted work; priority (choice 3) just picks the loser deterministically. NOLOCK (choice 4) doesn't apply to the conflicting writes and risks dirty reads. Eliminating the cycle by ordering access identically in both procedures removes the deadlock class entirely. Correct: consistent access order.

scenarios.title: Blocking: reports vs OLTP
scenarios.situation: A 10-minute financial report (READ COMMITTED) blocks order entry: writers wait on the report's shared locks.
evidence: order INSERTs time out during the report run
report needs point-in-time consistency, not live data
choices: Enable SNAPSHOT isolation and run the report under it: readers get a committed snapshot, writers never block
Run the report with NOLOCK
Kill the report during business hours
Raise the report to SERIALIZABLE
scenarios.hint: Does the report need live rows, or a consistent as-of view?
scenarios.why: SNAPSHOT gives the report a transactionally consistent view as of its start without taking shared locks — writers proceed untouched. It needs the version store enabled (tempdb sizing is the operational cost). Choice 2 (NOLOCK) risks dirty reads and allocation-order anomalies in a financial report — unacceptable. Choice 3 is avoidance. Choice 4 maximizes blocking. Correct: SNAPSHOT for the reporting workload.

scenarios.title: Million-row migration in one transaction
scenarios.situation: A data migration updates 3M rows in one transaction. The log fills, the transaction rolls back after 4 hours, and the job restarts from zero.
evidence: log full → 4 hours wasted, zero progress
choices: Chunk into batches (e.g., 5,000 rows) with a watermark column; each batch its own transaction; resume from the watermark
Grow the log file and retry the single transaction
Set the database to SIMPLE recovery during migration
Run the migration single-threaded to reduce log pressure
scenarios.hint: What unit of work can fail without losing everything?
scenarios.why: Chunking bounds each transaction's log and lock footprint; the watermark (migrated flag / processed key range) makes the job idempotent and resumable — a crash loses one batch, not 4 hours. Choice 2 just delays the same failure. Choice 3 breaks the recovery chain and is often unacceptable. Choice 4 doesn't fix log growth. Correct: batched, watermarked, resumable.

scenarios.title: Lost updates on shared records
scenarios.situation: Two admins edit the same product record; the second save silently overwrites the first. No concurrency control exists.
evidence: UPDATE products SET price=@p WHERE id=@id — last writer wins silently
pricing changes vanish without a trace
choices: Optimistic concurrency: read rowversion with the row; UPDATE ... WHERE id=@id AND rowversion=@rv; on @@ROWCOUNT=0 reload and prompt to merge
Lock the row with UPDLOCK while the admin edits
Add a 'last_modified' datetime check
Serialize all admin edits through a queue
scenarios.hint: How can the UPDATE itself detect that the row changed?
scenarios.why: The rowversion check makes the write conditional on 'nobody changed this since I read it' — conflicts become explicit instead of silent. No locks are held during the (long) human edit. Choice 2 holds locks for minutes — a blocking disaster. Choice 3 (datetime) has resolution and clock issues; rowversion is designed exactly for this. Choice 4 is heavy machinery for a solved problem. Correct: rowversion optimistic check.

scenarios.title: Partial rollback with savepoints
scenarios.situation: An order import processes header + 50 lines per order in one transaction. One bad line aborts the entire order; the business wants good lines kept.
evidence: single transaction; any line error → ROLLBACK all
keep valid lines, quarantine bad ones, continue the import
choices: SAVEPOINT per line: SAVE TRAN line_sp before each line; on line error ROLLBACK TRAN line_sp, log the bad line, continue
One transaction per line (50 commits per order)
Skip TRY/CATCH and let the import fail fast
Validate all lines before starting the transaction
scenarios.hint: What transaction feature undoes part of the work but not all?
scenarios.why: Savepoints give sub-transaction granularity: rolling back to the savepoint undoes only the bad line, the outer transaction (and good lines) survive. The bad line is logged to a quarantine table for review. Choice 2 works but 50 commits per order is needless overhead and breaks the order's atomicity. Choice 3 abandons the requirement. Choice 4 is good practice AND should be done, but data errors still occur — savepoints handle the residual. Correct: savepoint per line.

domains.name: Security & Access Control
domains.description: Least privilege, GRANT/REVOKE, SQL injection defense, masking, and auditing.

scenarios.title: App login with db_owner
scenarios.situation: The web app's SQL login is db_owner 'so deployments don't hit permission errors'. A recent XSS bug has the team worried.
evidence: any SQL injection now runs as database owner
choices: Split duties: app login gets EXECUTE on procedures + SELECT on views only; a separate deploy login owns schema changes
Keep db_owner but add a WAF in front
Rename the login to obscure it
Move permission checks into application code
scenarios.hint: If injection happens tonight, what can the login do?
scenarios.why: Least privilege bounds the blast radius: an injected query running as a procedure-only login can only do what the procedures allow — no ad-hoc DROP TABLE, no direct writes to sensitive tables. Ownership chaining makes this ergonomic (grant EXECUTE, not table access). Choice 2's WAF is defense-in-depth, not a substitute. Choice 3 is security by obscurity. Choice 4 duplicates what the database enforces better. Correct: role-separated, minimal grants.

scenarios.title: Injection via dynamic search procedure
scenarios.situation: A search procedure builds SQL by concatenating @term: EXEC('SELECT ... WHERE name LIKE ''%' + @term + '%'''). A pen test flagged it.
choices: Parameterize with sp_executesql: pass @term as a parameter, concatenating only the wildcards in the parameter value
Strip quotes and semicolons from @term first
Grant the caller fewer permissions
Move the LIKE to the application layer
scenarios.hint: Where does @term cross from data into code?
scenarios.why: sp_executesql with a real parameter keeps @term as data — it can never become syntax, no matter what it contains. The wildcards are added to the parameter value ('%' + @term + '%'), not to the SQL text. Choice 2 (blocklists) is the classic losing game. Choice 3 limits damage but leaves the hole. Choice 4 dodges the question. Correct: parameterize.

scenarios.title: Multi-tenant data leak
scenarios.situation: A SaaS app filters tenant rows in application code. A new reporting tool queries the database directly and exposes other tenants' data.
evidence: WHERE tenant_id = @t in every app query
direct-query reporting tool has no tenant filter
choices: Row-level security policy: FILTER PREDICATE on tenant_id = SESSION_CONTEXT value, enforced by the engine for every query path
Add the tenant filter to the reporting tool's queries
Create one database per tenant
Revoke the reporting tool's access
scenarios.hint: Which layer sees every query regardless of which tool sent it?
scenarios.why: Application-enforced filters only protect the paths that remember them — every new tool is a new chance to forget. RLS moves enforcement into the engine: the predicate applies to ad-hoc queries, ORMs, and reporting tools identically. Choice 2 repeats the original mistake on a new path. Choice 3 is a massive migration for a policy problem. Choice 4 kills the reporting use case. Correct: engine-enforced RLS.

scenarios.title: PII exposure in support tooling
scenarios.situation: Support staff need order history but keep copying full customer emails and phone numbers into tickets.
evidence: support: order dates, totals, status — not contact PII
PII pasted into ticket system weekly
choices: Dynamic data masking on email/phone for the support role: they see a***@**** while privileged roles see full values; stored data unchanged
Encrypt the columns with Always Encrypted
Tell support to stop copying PII
Create a separate support database
scenarios.hint: Can you hide the values from one role without changing what's stored?
scenarios.why: Masking is presentation-layer protection: the same query returns masked values to the support role and full values to privileged roles, with zero app changes and zero stored-data changes. It directly stops the copy-paste exposure. Choice 2 (Always Encrypted) is stronger but heavier — and would block legitimate privileged reads without app key handling. Choice 3 is policy without enforcement. Choice 4 duplicates infrastructure. Correct: dynamic data masking by role.

scenarios.title: Who changed the ledger?
scenarios.situation: Finance found altered ledger rows. Nobody knows who changed them or when — no audit trail exists.
evidence: zero record of DML on financial tables
prove who/when/what for every ledger change
choices: Database audit specification capturing UPDATE/DELETE on ledger tables to a protected file target, plus an application audit table with old/new values
Enable Change Data Capture only
Add updated_by/updated_at columns to the ledger
Restrict ledger access to one login
scenarios.hint: What proves the change happened — even to someone who can edit the table?
scenarios.why: The audit spec gives tamper-evident, engine-level proof (login, timestamp, statement) written outside the database; the application audit table adds business context (old vs new values, reason codes) the engine can't narrate. Choice 2 (CDC) captures changes but is designed for ETL, not security audit, and is mutable by db owners. Choice 3 is forgeable by anyone with write access. Choice 4 reduces suspects but proves nothing. Correct: layered audit — engine spec + app history.

scenarios.title: DENY vs REVOKE confusion
scenarios.situation: A contractor in two roles must be blocked from deleting orders. One role grants DELETE; an admin ran REVOKE and the contractor can still delete.
evidence: contractor in data_entry (grants DELETE) and reporting (no DELETE)
REVOKE DELETE ... FROM reporting — contractor still deletes
choices: DENY DELETE ON dbo.orders TO contractor (or to a role they're in): DENY overrides all GRANTs
REVOKE DELETE from data_entry instead
Remove the contractor from data_entry
REVOKE is enough; wait for cache refresh
scenarios.hint: Does REVOKE remove grants held via other roles?
scenarios.why: REVOKE only removes a grant from the named principal — the data_entry grant still stands, so the contractor still deletes. DENY is the explicit prohibition and wins over every GRANT from every role. Choice 2 would work but changes the role for all its members. Choice 3 also works but may break their legitimate duties. Choice 4 misunderstands: there's no cache, the grant genuinely remains. Correct: DENY.

scenarios.title: Ownership chaining for safe access
scenarios.situation: The app needs to place orders but must never touch the orders table directly. Direct grants feel wrong.
evidence: app places orders; no direct table writes
dbo.PlaceOrder procedure, dbo.orders table — same owner
choices: Grant the app EXECUTE on dbo.PlaceOrder only: ownership chaining lets the procedure write dbo.orders without any direct table grant
Grant INSERT on orders and validate in the app
Use an INSTEAD OF trigger for validation
Give the app SELECT and have it call a web service for writes
scenarios.hint: If procedure and table share an owner, which permission does the caller actually need?
scenarios.why: When procedure and table share an owner, the engine checks only the EXECUTE permission — the procedure becomes a controlled gate: it validates, writes, and logs, while the app login holds zero direct table rights. Choice 2 hands the app raw write access. Choice 3 adds complexity without removing the grant problem. Choice 4 is architecture astronautics for a solved database feature. Correct: EXECUTE-only via ownership chaining.

domains.name: Data Modeling & Normalization
domains.description: ER design, normal forms, keys and constraints, denormalization, and SCDs.

scenarios.title: Finding the normalization violation
scenarios.situation: An orders table stores customer_name and customer_email on every row. Renames require updating thousands of rows and reports disagree.
evidence: rename customer → 4,000 row updates; one missed → conflicting reports
choices: Normalize: customers(id, name, email); orders keeps customer_id FK only — each fact stored once
Add a trigger to sync the name across rows
Create a view that picks the most common name
Index customer_name for faster updates
scenarios.hint: What does customer_name actually depend on — the order, or the customer?
scenarios.why: customer_name depends on customer_id, not on the order — a transitive dependency violating 3NF. Storing it once in customers and referencing via FK makes renames a single-row update and contradictions impossible. Choice 2 (trigger sync) mechanizes the anomaly instead of removing it. Choice 3 papers over conflicting data. Choice 4 speeds up the wrong design. Correct: normalize to 3NF.

scenarios.title: Modeling the M:N relationship
scenarios.situation: Students enroll in courses. The current design has course1..course5 columns on the student table; course6 just arrived.
evidence: students(id, name, course1, course2, course3, course4, course5)
adding course6 = schema change; 'students in course X' needs 5 ORs
choices: Junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id, enrolled_on) with composite PK — M:N resolved properly
Add course6..course10 columns now to get ahead
Store course ids as a comma-separated list
One row per student-course pair in the students table
scenarios.hint: What database structure represents 'many-to-many' without numbered columns?
scenarios.why: Repeating groups violate 1NF and cap the relationship at an arbitrary number. A junction table models M:N natively: unlimited enrollments, enrolled_on lives on the relationship, the composite PK prevents duplicates, and queries are simple joins. Choice 2 repeats the mistake bigger. Choice 3 destroys queryability and integrity. Choice 4 duplicates student data (worse anomaly). Correct: junction table.

scenarios.title: The missing foreign key
scenarios.situation: The app 'enforces' referential integrity. The warehouse is full of orphaned order lines pointing at deleted products.
evidence: 12,000 line_items with product_id matching no product
choices: Add the FOREIGN KEY constraints (after cleaning orphans); let the engine enforce integrity for every writer, forever
Add more app-side checks
Schedule a nightly orphan-cleanup job
Make product deletes soft deletes only
scenarios.hint: Which writers does app-side checking protect against — and which does it miss?
scenarios.why: Application-enforced integrity protects only the paths that remember to check — bulk loads, new tools, and bugs all bypass it. Declarative FKs enforce for every writer including future ones, document the relationship, and help the optimizer. Choice 2 repeats the original failure mode. Choice 3 treats the symptom on a delay. Choice 4 is a fine policy but doesn't enforce anything by itself. Correct: real FOREIGN KEYs.

scenarios.title: Denormalization with a refresh contract
scenarios.situation: A dashboard aggregates 200M order rows on every refresh (45s). The team proposes storing order_count on the customer row, updated by the app.
evidence: customer.order_count maintained by app code on each order
choices: Denormalize deliberately: a summary table refreshed by a scheduled job with a reconciliation check — documented source, schedule, and drift detection
Update order_count in app code on every order insert
Add more indexes and hope the 45s drops
Cache the dashboard in the browser
scenarios.hint: How many code paths write orders — and will all of them remember the counter?
scenarios.why: App-maintained counters drift the first time any write path forgets the increment (bulk loads, backfills, new services). A job-refreshed summary table has one writer, a schedule, and a reconciliation query proving it matches source — the refresh contract. Choice 2 is exactly the drift-prone pattern. Choice 3 won't fix a 200M-row aggregation. Choice 4 hides stale data without defining staleness. Correct: denormalize with an explicit refresh contract.

scenarios.title: Customer history for the auditors
scenarios.situation: Regulators ask: 'what segment was customer X in on March 3rd?' The customer table overwrites segment in place — history is unknowable.
evidence: point-in-time segment for any past date
choices: Type 2 SCD: new row per segment change with eff_from/eff_to; 'as of' queries filter the date range
Add a segment_history audit table queried separately
Restore from backups to answer each question
Add previous_segment column (Type 3)
scenarios.hint: What schema lets you ask 'as of any date' with a single predicate?
scenarios.why: Type 2 makes history a first-class query: WHERE @asof BETWEEN eff_from AND eff_to returns the version current on any date, reproducibly. Choice 2 (separate audit table) works but splits the model and complicates every temporal query. Choice 3 is operationally absurd. Choice 4 (Type 3) answers only 'current vs previous', not arbitrary dates. Correct: Type 2 effective-dated rows.

scenarios.title: Natural vs surrogate keys
scenarios.situation: The schema uses email as the customer PRIMARY KEY. Users now want to change their email addresses, and email is referenced by 12 tables.
evidence: customers(email PK); 12 FK tables reference email
choices: Surrogate IDENTITY PK; email becomes UNIQUE NOT NULL; FKs reference the stable id — email changes touch one row
Cascading updates on all 12 FKs
Disallow email changes
Composite PK (email, created_at)
scenarios.hint: What should happen — physically — when a user's email changes?
scenarios.why: Natural keys carry meaning, and meaning changes: every email change would cascade across 12 tables (locking, log, risk). A surrogate key never changes; the email becomes a unique attribute — renames are one-row updates. Choice 2 works mechanically but turns a trivial update into a 13-table distributed write. Choice 3 fights the business. Choice 4 keeps the instability. Correct: surrogate PK, unique natural key.

scenarios.title: Optional relationships: NULL or not?
scenarios.situation: Orders may have a coupon. The design stores coupon_code NULL on most rows; analysts keep tripping over NULL semantics in reports.
evidence: orders(..., coupon_code VARCHAR(20) NULL) — null on 92% of rows
analysts' GROUP BY coupon_code shows a giant NULL bucket; joins misbehave
scenarios.prompt: What is the better design conversation?
choices: Keep the nullable FK if 'no coupon' is genuinely the common case, but expose analysts a view that translates NULL → 'NO_COUPON' — or model redemptions as a separate 1:N table if coupons gain attributes
Make coupon_code NOT NULL with a dummy 'NONE' coupon row
Split into two tables: orders and coupon_orders
Remove coupons from the model entirely
scenarios.hint: Is the pain in the model, or in how consumers see the NULL?
scenarios.why: The NULL is honest (most orders have no coupon), but raw NULLs confuse consumers — a view translating NULL to 'NO_COUPON' keeps the model clean and reports sane. If coupons grow attributes (discount, campaign), a separate redemption table (order_id, coupon_id) is the proper 1:N. Choice 2's dummy row pollutes the coupon dimension. Choice 3 splits tables without a reason. Choice 4 deletes the business. Correct: nullable FK + consumer-friendly view, or a redemption table when attributes grow.

domains.name: Advanced SQL Patterns
domains.description: Recursive CTEs, pivots, JSON handling, MERGE, and classic analytic patterns.

scenarios.title: Bill of materials explosion
scenarios.situation: Manufacturing needs the full component tree under each assembly — assemblies contain sub-assemblies to arbitrary depth. The app loops in code.
evidence: parts(id, name, parent_assembly_id) — adjacency list, depth varies
application recursion: N queries per assembly
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct query approach?
choices: Recursive CTE: anchor on top assemblies, recursive member joins children, depth guard + MAXRECURSION
Five chained self joins (max depth 5)
A WHILE loop in T-SQL inserting into a temp table
Flatten the hierarchy into the app and cache it
scenarios.hint: Which SQL construct iterates a join until no new rows appear?
scenarios.why: The recursive CTE expresses arbitrary-depth traversal in one set-based statement: anchor selects roots, the recursive member appends each level, and the lvl guard plus MAXRECURSION protect against cyclic data. Choice 2 breaks at depth 6. Choice 3 reinvents the CTE worse (row-by-row, no optimizer). Choice 4 moves the problem without solving it. Correct: recursive CTE.

scenarios.title: Monthly sales as columns
scenarios.situation: Finance wants one row per region with a column per month. The app currently pivots 12 query results in code.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best SQL approach?
choices: Conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN MONTH(d)=1 THEN total END) AS Jan, ... — one pass, portable, explicit
PIVOT operator with a hardcoded month list
12 separate queries UNIONed
Return rows and let the BI tool pivot
scenarios.hint: Can a single GROUP BY produce twelve different sums?
scenarios.why: Conditional aggregation does the whole pivot in one scan with plain, portable SQL — each month is one expression, the logic is visible, and it works in every dialect. Choice 2 (PIVOT) also works but its syntax is dialect-specific and the mandatory IN-list is equally hardcoded. Choice 3 is 12 scans. Choice 4 is legitimate when a real BI tool exists, but the question asks for the SQL approach. Correct: conditional aggregation.

scenarios.title: Querying the JSON payloads
scenarios.situation: Order line items arrive as a JSON array in one column. Analysts need sku/qty as rows for joining to the catalog.
evidence: rows of (order_id, sku, qty) joinable to products
choices: CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(items_json) WITH (sku VARCHAR(20) '$.sku', qty INT '$.qty') — typed relational rows per order
JSON_VALUE(items_json, '$[0].sku') for each array position
Store the JSON pre-shredded by the app instead
LIKE '%"sku":"A1"%' searches
scenarios.hint: Which function turns a JSON array into a rowset?
scenarios.why: OPENJSON with an explicit WITH schema shreds each document's array into typed rows, correlated per order via CROSS APPLY — the result joins and aggregates like any table. Choice 2 handles only fixed positions and explodes with variable-length arrays. Choice 3 is a fine architecture but doesn't answer the SQL question. Choice 4 is a correctness nightmare. Correct: OPENJSON shredding.

scenarios.title: Nightly catalog sync
scenarios.situation: A nightly job syncs 500k products from a vendor feed: update changed, insert new. Two concurrent runs once double-inserted the same sku.
evidence: concurrent runs both INSERTed sku X — duplicates
choices: MERGE ... WITH (HOLDLOCK) on the key, or the UPDATE/INSERT pair inside a SERIALIZABLE transaction — serialize the key range so only one session inserts
Add a unique constraint and let one run fail
Run the job single-threaded via a lock file
DELETE all then INSERT all each night
scenarios.hint: What happens between the 'check' and the 'act' under concurrency?
scenarios.why: The race is check-then-act: both sessions find no row, both insert. HOLDLOCK (serializable) on the MERGE target holds the key range through the statement, so the second session blocks until the first commits, then sees the row and updates. Choice 2 (unique constraint) prevents duplicates but turns the loser into an error — the sync is still broken. Choice 3 works operationally but serializes the whole job. Choice 4 is downtime-adjacent and loses history. Correct: serialized upsert.

scenarios.title: Finding coverage gaps
scenarios.situation: Support contracts need contiguous coverage: find gaps in per-customer coverage periods (start/end dates) to flag uninsured days.
evidence: coverage(customer_id, start_date, end_date) — multiple rows per customer
date ranges with no coverage, per customer
choices: Islands of coverage via grouped row-number arithmetic, then look for gaps between island boundaries (MAX(end) < next MIN(start))
A calendar table LEFT JOINed to coverage, filtering NULLs
Cursor over each customer's periods comparing dates
DATEDIFF between consecutive rows with LAG
scenarios.hint: First merge overlapping periods into continuous blocks — then what's a gap?
scenarios.why: The islands technique collapses overlapping/contiguous periods per customer into continuous coverage blocks; gaps are where one island's end < the next island's start. Choice 2 (calendar join) also works and is arguably simpler to read — but on multi-year ranges per customer it's far more expensive; the islands approach is the set-based classic. Choice 3 is row-by-row. Choice 4's LAG only compares adjacent raw rows, missing overlaps that merge periods. Correct: islands then gap detection.

scenarios.title: Top product per category, ties included
scenarios.situation: Marketing wants the top-selling product per category — including ties. ROW_NUMBER gives exactly one even when two tie for first.
evidence: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) rn ... WHERE rn=1
choices: RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(): tied top sellers share rank 1 and all satisfy r=1
DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER()
Remove the filter and sort by sales DESC
Add a tie-breaker to the ROW_NUMBER ORDER BY
scenarios.hint: Which ranking function gives ties the same number?
scenarios.why: RANK() assigns equal values the same rank, so all tied leaders get rank 1 and pass the r=1 filter — exactly the 'ties included' requirement. Choice 2 (DENSE_RANK) behaves identically here (no gaps matter at rank 1), but RANK is the conventional choice. Choice 3 returns everything. Choice 4 (tie-breaker) does the opposite of what's asked — it arbitrarily excludes. Correct: RANK().

scenarios.title: Running total that resets monthly
scenarios.situation: Finance wants a running revenue total that resets each month — the current query accumulates across the whole year.
evidence: SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
cumulative within each month, resetting on the 1st
choices: PARTITION BY month: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(day), MONTH(day) ORDER BY day)
Add a CASE resetting to 0 on the first of the month
GROUP BY month first, then window over the groups
Use a cursor resetting a variable monthly
scenarios.hint: What restarts a window function's frame?
scenarios.why: PARTITION BY restarts the window frame for each month: the running total accumulates within the partition only. The ORDER BY inside keeps day order. lessons.title: Queries — Core concepts
concepts: Logical query order: sQL's logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > @last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n) is stable under churn and faster on deep pages (no scanning skipped rows).
Alias scope: WHERE executes before the SELECT list, so the alias doesn't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after, so it does.
OFFSET/FETCH is simple and fine for static data.

example.code:
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY product_id
OFFSET 40 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;
example.walkthrough: OFFSET counts rows from the current result start — concurrent inserts/deletes shift everything, causing duplicates/skips across pages. Choose by data volatility.

pitfalls: Common trap: use = instead of LIKE for patterns.
Common trap: use the alias in GROUP BY instead.
Common trap: order doesn't matter for pages.
Common trap: they are identical; UNION is shorter to type.

lessons.title: Aggregations — Core concepts
concepts: GROUP BY grain: aggregation grain must match the question's grain: order_lines has one row per line item, so COUNT(*) counts lines, not orders. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY computes them.

Aggregation correctness: the #1 aggregation bug is grouping at the wrong grain — always ask 'what is one row here?' before trusting a COUNT. Conditional aggregation puts CASE inside the aggregate — one scan produces all three columns.
Aggregates and NULLs: all aggregates except COUNT(*) skip NULLs: AVG(5, NULL, NULL) = 5, not 1.67. (COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULLs — usually what you want for 'unique'.).

GROUPING SETS lists multiple groupings computed in one pass: ((region,quarter),(region),()) gives detail rows, region subtotals, and the grand total. WHERE filters input rows before grouping — aggregates don't exist yet.
ROLLUP(region, quarter) gives the hierarchical chain; CUBE gives all combinations.

example.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM order_lines GROUP BY customer_id; -- inflated vs known order counts
example.walkthrough: Aggregation grain must match the question's grain: order_lines has one row per line item, so COUNT(*) counts lines, not orders. Fix: COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), or aggregate orders (one row per order) instead.

pitfalls: Common trap: conditional aggregation requires dynamic SQL.
Common trap: add more columns to GROUP BY until the numbers look right.
Common trap: GROUP BY with multiple columns gives subtotals automatically.
Common trap: the query is wrong; averages can't use NULLs at all.

lessons.title: Joins — Core concepts
concepts: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows, extending missing matches with NULLs — but WHERE o.status='shipped' then rejects those NULL rows (UNKNOWN ≠ TRUE), silently converting the outer join to an inner join. LEFT JOIN preserves top-level rows with no manager (NULL manager name).
Predicate placement: NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe (correlated predicate per row) and short-circuits.
Fanout: whenever totals look multiplied, check join fanout first.

Join grain: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched pairs plus unmatched rows from both sides (NULLs where the other side is missing) — the reconciliation shape in one query. A self join aliases the table twice (e, m) so it plays both roles: employee row and manager row.
Anti-joins: rule: for anti-joins, NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN/IS NULL; treat NOT IN as guilty until proven NULL-free.

example.code:
SELECT * FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS
 (SELECT 1 FROM order_lines ol WHERE ol.product_id = p.product_id);
example.walkthrough: NOT IN (subquery with NULL) → every comparison is UNKNOWN → zero rows. WHERE right.id IS NULL is equivalent and sometimes clearer.

pitfalls: Common trap: fanout only happens with FULL JOIN.
Common trap: LEFT JOIN is broken in SQL Server.
Common trap: self joins require temp tables.
Common trap: UNION of two LEFT JOINs.

lessons.title: Window Functions — Core concepts
concepts: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows within each department; the outer filter rn=1 keeps each department's top earner with all columns. ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3 — unique, arbitrary among ties.
PARTITION BY: lAG(expr) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY day) returns the previous row's value within each product's timeline — no self-join, no date arithmetic, handles gaps naturally.
Top-N per group: GROUP BY + MAX needs a self-join to recover the row. GROUP BY is for collapsing; OVER() is for annotating.

Window frames: the default window frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — RANGE treats tied ORDER BY values as peers, giving them identical results. That's the window function superpower: aggregates at any grain alongside detail rows.
ROWS vs RANGE: know your frame: ROWS = physical, RANGE = logical peers.

example.walkthrough: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows within each department; the outer filter rn=1 keeps each department's top earner with all columns. RANK()/DENSE_RANK() differ on ties: ROW_NUMBER is arbitrary among ties, RANK skips numbers, DENSE_RANK doesn't.

pitfalls: Common trap: window functions require GROUP BY.
Common trap: GROUP BY dept with MAX(salary).
Common trap: GROUP BY with the average joined back.
Common trap: LAST_VALUE works with the default frame.

lessons.title: T-SQL Programming — Core concepts
concepts: TRY/CATCH + explicit transaction: on error, CATCH rolls back the open transaction (@@TRANCOUNT check) and THROW re-raises the original error with its number/line — the caller gets truth, not a masked message.
Transaction control: SET XACT_ABORT ON makes most runtime errors abort the batch and roll back the transaction — fail-atomic instead of fail-partial. Never leave a transaction half-committed.
Temp tables: functions: callable inline in queries, must be side-effect-free (no DML on base tables, deterministic preferred) — perfect for 'calculate discount'.

example.code:
DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = @s';
EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N'@s VARCHAR(20)', @s = @status;
example.walkthrough: sp_executesql with declared parameters keeps input as data — parameterized, injection-proof, with reusable plans. EXEC(@string) with concatenation lets input become code (classic injection). Dynamic SQL is legitimate for optional-filter searches; just parameterize it.

pitfalls: Common trap: NOCOUNT breaks result sets.
Common trap: use functions for ETL workflows.
Common trap: @@ERROR checks after every statement.
Common trap: simplest and safe if you trust the input.

lessons.title: Performance — Core concepts
concepts: Index seeks: a covering index includes all columns the query needs: key columns (customer_id, order_date) support the seek; INCLUDE (total) carries the payload without widening the key. Sargable = Search ARGument ABLE: the optimizer can seek the index when the column appears bare in a range/equality predicate.
Execution plans: on first execution, SQL Server 'sniffs' the parameter values and compiles a plan optimal for them, then reuses it for all values.
Statistics: estimated vs actual row counts: a big gap = the optimizer decided on bad cardinality — usually stale/missing statistics (UPDATE STATISTICS) or skewed data needing filtered stats.
Plan caching: a single set-based UPDATE...FROM processes all rows in one plan, one pass. The plan names the operators (seek vs scan, loop vs hash vs merge join); the row-count gap names the cause.

example.code:
-- slow: WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026
-- fast: WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'
example.walkthrough: Sargable = Search ARGument ABLE: the optimizer can seek the index when the column appears bare in a range/equality predicate. Wrapping it in YEAR() hides the value — every row must be computed and compared (scan). Rewrite as a range on the bare column.

pitfalls: Common trap: INCLUDE columns are searchable in seeks.
Common trap: indexes work the same with functions on columns.
Common trap: WHILE loops with temp tables beat set operations.
Common trap: add the index the missing-index hint suggests.

lessons.title: SQL — Core concepts
concepts: JOIN type declares which rows survive: INNER keeps only matches, LEFT keeps every row from the left table (NULLs where nothing matched), and choosing wrong silently drops or duplicates rows.

Indexes are lookup structures, not magic. A B-tree on the filtered/joined column turns a full scan into a seek — but only for selective predicates; the planner ignores indexes when it must read most of the table anyway.
Window functions (OVER / PARTITION BY) compute aggregates across related rows without collapsing them — ranking, running totals, and per-group averages on detail rows are their home turf.

Transactions are atomic, consistent, isolated, durable — but isolation levels are a spectrum. READ COMMITTED still permits lost updates; serialize check-and-set logic with row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or atomic conditional writes.
EXPLAIN is the truth serum: read actual rows vs estimates, spot nested loops with huge inner loop counts, and fix stale statistics (ANALYZE) before redesigning queries.
Write for the planner: sargable predicates (no functions on indexed columns in WHERE), covering indexes for hot queries, and pagination with keyset (WHERE id > ?) instead of deep OFFSET.

example.code:
SELECT name,
       salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM employees;
example.walkthrough: The window functions compute per-department average and rank on every employee row — no GROUP BY, no collapsed rows. PARTITION BY slices the window by department; ORDER BY inside OVER defines the ranking order.

pitfalls: Common trap: INNER JOIN when you need 'all X including those with no Y' — unmatched rows silently vanish; reach for LEFT JOIN.
Common trap: wrapping an indexed column in a function in WHERE (WHERE YEAR(created)=2026) — defeats the index; use a range predicate instead.
Common trap: assuming READ COMMITTED prevents concurrent check-then-act races — it does not; lock the row or make the write conditional.
Common trap: SELECT * in hot queries — it blocks index-only scans and drags unneeded columns over the wire; select exactly what you need.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Sql move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: Welcome: how this CBT is built
concepts: This bootcamp is organized into domains (indexing, transactions, security, modeling, advanced patterns), each with lessons, scenario drills, and hands-on labs. Work domains in order the first time; later, target your weakest areas.
Lessons teach a concept with a worked example; scenarios put you in a realistic incident or review and ask you to choose the best action; labs have you run commands yourself.
The mock-assessment domain assembles scenarios from every domain into a timed run — save it for the end of each study cycle.
Progress is cumulative: concepts from early domains (logical query order, joins) are assumed knowledge in later ones (indexing, transactions).

example.code:
-- Your first checkpoint: can you read this and explain what each clause does?
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.region = 'West'
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 5
ORDER BY orders DESC;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: FROM+JOIN build the working set; WHERE filters rows before grouping; GROUP BY collapses per customer; HAVING filters groups; SELECT projects; ORDER BY sorts. If you can narrate this pipeline, you are ready for domain 1.

pitfalls: Jumping straight to the mock assessment before doing the lessons
Memorizing syntax without understanding the logical pipeline
Skipping labs — scenarios test recognition, labs test doing

lessons.title: Study strategy: spaced, mixed, and applied
concepts: Spaced repetition beats cramming: revisit each domain's lessons 1 day, 3 days, and 7 days after first contact. The bootcamp's domain order is your review schedule.
Interleave domains: after finishing joins, do a few window-function scenarios before moving on. Mixing forces discrimination — exactly what interviews test.
Every lesson ends with a try-it prompt: actually run the SQL. Retrieval practice (writing the query from memory) builds durable skill; re-reading does not.
Track your misses: when a scenario's 'why' surprises you, re-do that domain's lab before moving on.

example.code:
-- Build a study loop, not a reading list:
-- Day 1: Lessons + scenarios for one domain
-- Day 2: Labs for that domain + 5 scenarios from the previous domain
-- Day 7: Mock assessment mixing all domains so far
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the loop alternates learning (lessons), application (scenarios), and doing (labs), with built-in spaced review. Adjust the pace, not the pattern.

pitfalls: Reading all lessons first and doing scenarios 'later'
Doing scenarios once and never revisiting the ones you missed
Confusing familiarity ('I recognize this') with ability ('I can write it cold')

lessons.title: What SQL interviews and assessments actually test
concepts: Interviewers test reasoning, not recall: they want to hear you narrate the logical query pipeline (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY) as you build a query.
The five classic live-coding tasks: top-N per group, running totals, gaps-and-islands, deduplication, and funnel/conversion analysis — all covered in the windows and advanced-sql domains.
Performance questions are scenario-based: 'this query is slow, the plan shows a scan — what do you check?' Know sargability, implicit conversions, and index design cold.
Behavioral SQL questions probe judgment: transactions and isolation choices, how you prevented injection, how you tuned a production query without breaking correctness.

example.code:
-- A typical interview prompt:
-- 'Find each customer's most recent order.'
-- Strong answer narrates: rank orders per customer with ROW_NUMBER()
-- partitioned by customer, ordered by date desc, filter rn = 1.
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the interviewer is listening for the plan (partition, order, filter) before the syntax. State the approach, then write it. If stuck, say what you would check (the plan, the indexes).

pitfalls: Writing code silently without narrating your plan
Reaching for cursors/loops where a set-based query fits
Saying 'add an index' without checking the plan first

lessons.title: Thinking in sets: the mental model behind everything
concepts: SQL operates on sets of rows, not loops over records. Every query describes the result set you want; the engine chooses how to produce it.
Joins build a combined set, WHERE/HAVING filter it, GROUP BY collapses it, window functions compute across it without collapsing — one mental model covers all four domains.
Correlated subqueries and cursors are the 'loop brain' leaking through: they usually work but scale badly. Prefer set operations (joins, window functions, EXISTS).
When a query confuses you, run it clause by clause: SELECT * FROM the FROM/JOIN first, add WHERE, then GROUP BY — watch the set shrink and reshape at each step.

example.code:
-- Compare: loop brain vs set brain
-- Loop brain: FOR EACH customer: run a query counting their orders  (N+1 queries)
-- Set brain: one GROUP BY over the join  (1 query)
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the set version lets the optimizer choose one efficient plan and touches each table once. N+1 patterns are the #1 SQL performance smell in application code.

pitfalls: Solving every problem with a correlated subquery
Forgetting that WHERE filters before grouping and HAVING after
Treating the database as a dumb store and doing aggregation in app code
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: SELECT essentials: projection, DISTINCT, TOP/LIMIT
concepts: Projection: SELECT lists exactly the columns the consumer needs. SELECT * is fine for exploration but a liability in production code (schema changes break consumers, extra I/O).
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across the whole select list, not one column — DISTINCT a, b dedupes (a,b) pairs.
TOP (T-SQL) / LIMIT (Postgres, MySQL) / FETCH FIRST cap rows; always pair with ORDER BY or the 'top N' is arbitrary.
Column aliases rename output; table aliases shorten references and are required for self joins. Alias in ORDER BY works (runs after SELECT); alias in WHERE does not.

example.code:
SELECT DISTINCT region FROM customers ORDER BY region
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: DISTINCT collapses duplicate regions; ORDER BY makes the result deterministic; FETCH caps at 10 rows. Without ORDER BY, which 10 rows you get is undefined.

pitfalls: SELECT * in application code and views
DISTINCT on one column expecting per-column dedupe
TOP/LIMIT without ORDER BY and assuming a stable result
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Filtering: WHERE, LIKE, BETWEEN, IN, and NULL
concepts: WHERE filters rows before any grouping or aggregation. Put the most selective, cheapest predicates first for readability; the optimizer reorders anyway.
NULL is not a value: = NULL never matches — use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns zero rows (three-valued logic trap).
LIKE patterns: % multi-char, _ single-char. Leading wildcards ('%term') defeat B-tree seeks; prefer full-text search for contains-searches.
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends; for dates prefer >= start AND < day-after-end to avoid time-component bugs.

example.code:
SELECT id, name FROM products
WHERE discontinued IS NULL
  AND (name LIKE 'Pro%' OR sku IN ('A-100','B-200'))
  AND price BETWEEN 10 AND 50;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: IS NULL handles the nullable flag correctly; LIKE 'Pro%' is sargable (seeks); BETWEEN 10 AND 50 includes both endpoints. Each predicate narrows the set before it reaches SELECT.

pitfalls: = NULL instead of IS NULL
NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL
BETWEEN on datetimes missing end-of-day rows
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Sorting and pagination that survives production
concepts: ORDER BY is the only guarantee of row order — without it, the engine may return rows in any order, and that order can change between runs.
Keyset pagination (WHERE id > @last ORDER BY id LIMIT n) is stable under concurrent inserts/deletes and O(1) on deep pages; OFFSET re-scans skipped rows every time.
Tie-breakers matter: ORDER BY created_at alone is unstable for equal timestamps — append the PK (ORDER BY created_at, id) for deterministic pages.
Sorts are expensive: ORDER BY on an unindexed expression forces a sort operator. Index the sort key or rethink whether the client needs server-side sorting.

example.code:
-- Keyset pagination: stable, fast on deep pages
SELECT id, name FROM products
WHERE id > @last_seen_id
ORDER BY id
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the WHERE clause seeks directly to the resume point via the PK index — no counting past 40,000 skipped rows. @last_seen_id comes from the previous page's final row.

pitfalls: OFFSET pagination on large, churning tables
ORDER BY a non-unique column with no tie-breaker
Assuming result order without ORDER BY because 'it always came back sorted'
lessons.try_it: Try it now in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Set operations: UNION, EXCEPT, INTERSECT
concepts: UNION ALL concatenates result sets (fast, keeps duplicates); UNION dedupes (adds a sort/distinct — cost you pay only when you need it).
Both sides must have the same number of columns with compatible types; column names come from the first query.
EXCEPT returns rows in the first set not in the second; INTERSECT returns rows in both — NULLs are treated as equal for set-operation comparison (unlike =).
Prefer UNION ALL + explicit dedupe logic when you know the sources are disjoint — you skip the hidden sort.

example.code:
-- Combine active and archived orders, then remove any already refunded
SELECT id, total FROM orders
UNION ALL
SELECT id, total FROM orders_archive
EXCEPT
SELECT order_id, total FROM refunds;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: UNION ALL is correct because an order lives in exactly one of the two tables (no dupes to remove, no wasted sort). EXCEPT then strips refunded orders. Names/types align positionally.

pitfalls: UNION where UNION ALL would do (paying for a sort you don't need)
Mismatched column counts/types across the set operator
Forgetting ORDER BY applies to the whole combined result, placed once at the end

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING: the aggregation pipeline
concepts: GROUP BY collapses rows sharing key values into one row per group; every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY (or be functionally dependent).
HAVING filters groups after aggregation — it can reference aggregates; WHERE cannot. Decide 'row filter or group filter?' before writing.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(DISTINCT col) dedupes first. Mixing them up is a classic wrong-answer generator.
Grouping on expressions is fine — GROUP BY YEAR(order_date) — but the expression must match the SELECT list (or use the alias in dialects that allow it in GROUP BY).

example.code:
SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS customers, AVG(order_total) AS avg_order
FROM customers
WHERE active = 1
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100
ORDER BY avg_order DESC;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: WHERE drops inactive customers first (cheaper), GROUP BY builds per-region buckets, HAVING keeps only regions with 100+ customers, SELECT computes the aggregates, ORDER BY ranks. Each clause sees the output of the previous one.

pitfalls: Putting aggregate conditions in WHERE
COUNT(col) when you meant COUNT(*) and silently dropping NULL rows
Selecting a non-grouped, non-aggregated column

lessons.title: Aggregate functions and NULL semantics
concepts: All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs: AVG of (10, NULL) is 10, not 5. Decide whether NULLs should be excluded or coalesced before aggregating.
MIN/MAX work on strings and dates too — handy for 'first/last' per group without a window function.
SUM of an empty set is NULL, COUNT of an empty set is 0 — guard dashboards with COALESCE(SUM(x),0).
Aggregates compose with CASE for conditional aggregation: one pass over the data produces many metrics.

example.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  COUNT(email) AS with_email,
  COALESCE(SUM(amount),0) AS revenue,
  MIN(created_at) AS first_seen
FROM customers;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: COUNT(email) skips NULL emails so with_email <= total; COALESCE turns an empty SUM into 0 for the dashboard; MIN(created_at) gives first-seen without sorting the whole table in app code.

pitfalls: Assuming AVG includes NULLs as zeros
Forgetting SUM over no rows is NULL, not 0
Running one query per metric instead of conditional aggregation

lessons.title: Conditional aggregation with CASE
concepts: CASE inside an aggregate computes per-group breakdowns in a single scan: SUM(CASE WHEN status='paid' THEN amount END) is one pass, not N queries.
The ELSE-less CASE returns NULL for non-matching rows, which aggregates ignore — exactly the behavior you want for conditional sums/counts.
Pivot-style reports (one column per month/status/channel) are conditional aggregation; reserve PIVOT syntax for when the tooling demands it.
Keep the CASE deterministic and sargable-friendly: compute on raw columns, not on function-wrapped ones, when the source query also filters.

example.code:
SELECT
  DATEPART(year, order_date) AS yr,
  SUM(CASE WHEN channel='web' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS web_rev,
  SUM(CASE WHEN channel='store' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS store_rev,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN total > 1000 THEN 1 END) AS big_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATEPART(year, order_date);
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: one scan, one GROUP BY, four metrics. ELSE 0 vs no-ELSE: with ELSE 0 the SUM includes zeros (same result); for COUNT the no-ELSE version counts only matches. Choose deliberately.

pitfalls: One query per breakdown column (N scans)
CASE returning 0 vs NULL without thinking about COUNT vs SUM
Putting the CASE in WHERE instead of inside the aggregate

lessons.title: ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS
concepts: GROUPING SETS lists exactly which group-by combinations to compute — subtotals and grand totals in one pass instead of UNION ALL of many queries.
ROLLUP (a,b) gives (a,b), (a), () — hierarchical subtotals for drill-down reports. CUBE (a,b) gives all 2^n combinations.
GROUPING(col) distinguishes a real NULL from a subtotal NULL in the output so reports can label 'All regions' correctly.
Use these for reporting layers, not hot OLTP paths: they multiply aggregation work, so schedule them in batch/warehouse workloads.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: one scan yields per-(region,channel) rows, per-region subtotals (channel NULL, g_reg=0... actually GROUPING(channel)=1), and the grand total. The report layer turns g_reg/g_chan flags into 'All' labels.

pitfalls: UNION ALL of separate GROUP BY queries instead of ROLLUP
Misreading subtotal NULLs as data NULLs
Running CUBE on high-cardinality columns and exploding the result

lessons.title: INNER and OUTER joins: matching vs preserving
concepts: INNER JOIN keeps only matching pairs; LEFT JOIN keeps every left row, filling NULLs where nothing matched. Choose by the question: 'which X have Y' vs 'all X, with their Y if any'.
RIGHT JOIN is LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped — standardize on LEFT for readability; FULL OUTER keeps non-matching rows from both sides (rare, mostly reconciliation).
The ON clause defines the match; the WHERE clause filters the joined result. For outer joins this distinction changes results — the #1 join bug.
Join on indexed, type-identical keys. Mismatched types (int vs varchar) force conversions and kill seek performance.

example.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'open'
WHERE c.region = 'West';
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the status predicate lives in ON so customers without open orders still appear (with NULL order_id). Move it to WHERE and the LEFT JOIN silently becomes an INNER JOIN — the classic bug.

pitfalls: Filtering the nullable side in WHERE, collapsing the outer join
RIGHT JOINs scattered through a query
Joining on mismatched types and wondering why it's slow

lessons.title: Self joins and non-equi joins
concepts: A self join treats one table as two roles (employee/manager) via two aliases — mandatory technique for hierarchies stored as adjacency lists.
Non-equi joins match on ranges/inequality: join events to the price tier whose range contains the amount, or pair each row with its predecessor.
Range joins can explode cardinality: verify the join produces the expected row count (a tier table with overlapping ranges duplicates rows).
For deep hierarchies prefer recursive CTEs over chained self joins; self joins shine at exactly one level (manager, previous row).

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: two aliases, one table. LEFT JOIN keeps the CEO (no manager) with a NULL manager name. The alias is what makes the single table play two roles.

pitfalls: Forgetting the second alias on a self join
Overlapping ranges in a non-equi join duplicating rows
Chaining 5 self joins instead of a recursive CTE

lessons.title: Semi and anti joins: EXISTS, IN, and their NULL traps
concepts: Semi join ('which customers have orders'): EXISTS or IN. Anti join ('which customers have NO orders'): NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL.
NOT IN is dangerous: one NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN and returns zero rows. NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe — prefer it.
EXISTS short-circuits on the first match and ignores the SELECT list (SELECT 1); the optimizer often turns it into an efficient semi-join operator.
For 'top per group' or 'latest per key', window functions usually beat correlated EXISTS on both clarity and performance.

example.code:
-- Customers with no orders, NULL-safe
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: NOT EXISTS checks the correlated condition per customer and stops at the first order found. Even if orders.customer_id contains NULLs, the logic stays correct — NOT IN would return nothing.

pitfalls: NOT IN against a nullable subquery
SELECT * inside EXISTS (works, but signals misunderstanding)
Correlated subquery where a window function is cleaner

lessons.title: Join order, cardinality, and performance
concepts: Logical joins are commutative to the optimizer, but cardinality mistakes are yours: joining through a many-to-many bridge without dedupe multiplies rows and inflates SUMs.
Fan-out check: after joining, compare row counts against the driving table. Unexpected growth means a join key isn't unique on one side.
Pre-aggregate before joining when you need per-key metrics: aggregate orders to one row per customer first, then join — avoids row multiplication entirely.
The optimizer picks join algorithms (nested loops / hash / merge) from statistics; stale stats cause bad picks, so keep them updated on churning tables.

example.code:
-- Safe pattern: aggregate first, then join (no fan-out)
SELECT c.name, s.total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS total_spent
           FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) s
  ON s.customer_id = c.id;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the derived table collapses orders to one row per customer before the join, so customer rows never duplicate and total_spent is exact. Joining raw orders then summing would need DISTINCT gymnastics.

pitfalls: Joining then SUMming across a fan-out (inflated totals)
Assuming a join key is unique without checking
Blaming the join type when stale statistics picked a bad plan

lessons.title: Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
concepts: Window functions compute across a set of related rows without collapsing them — every input row survives, with a computed column attached.
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups (like GROUP BY but non-collapsing); ORDER BY inside OVER defines the ranking order within each partition.
ROW_NUMBER is unique even with ties; RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,2,2,4); DENSE_RANK has no gaps (1,2,2,3). Pick by the business rule, not habit.
The #1 use: top-N per group — rank inside the partition, filter rn = 1 in an outer query (window functions can't appear in WHERE).

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: each customer's orders are numbered newest-first. Wrap this in a CTE and filter rn = 1 for 'latest order per customer' — one pass, no correlated subquery, correct with ties broken deterministically by adding id to the ORDER BY.

pitfalls: Using window functions in WHERE (not allowed — wrap in a subquery)
ROW_NUMBER when the spec needs RANK's tie behavior
Non-deterministic ORDER BY inside OVER (ties break randomly)

lessons.title: LAG, LEAD, and frame clauses
concepts: LAG/LEAD peek at previous/next rows within the partition — ideal for deltas: today vs yesterday, current vs previous status.
ROWS BETWEEN defines the frame physically (1 PRECEDING = the row above); RANGE defines it logically by value (peers with equal ORDER BY values all count).
Default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — with ties, RANGE includes all peers, which surprises people expecting one row.
FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE need explicit frames: LAST_VALUE with the default frame returns the current row, not the partition's last row.

example.code:
SELECT day, revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day,
  revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS delta
FROM daily_revenue;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: LAG fetches yesterday's revenue alongside today's; the delta is plain arithmetic. First row gets NULL delta — wrap in COALESCE if the report needs 0.

pitfalls: RANGE vs ROWS confusion with tied ORDER BY values
LAST_VALUE without an explicit frame
Forgetting LAG returns NULL at partition edges

lessons.title: Running totals and moving averages
concepts: A running total is SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) — cumulative without collapsing rows, perfect for burn-up charts.
Moving averages use a sliding frame: AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for a 7-day average.
ROWS (physical) vs RANGE (logical) matters at the edges: with duplicate dates, RANGE's 6 PRECEDING is value-based and can include more than 7 rows.
Partition the cumulative metric when it resets per group: SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY day) restarts the running total per region.

example.code:
SELECT day,
  SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total,
  AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_revenue;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the running total accumulates from the first row; the 7-day average slides. ROWS keeps the window exactly 7 physical rows even when dates repeat — use RANGE only when you want peer-inclusive logic.

pitfalls: Default frame surprises with LAST_VALUE/FIRST_VALUE
RANGE frames on non-unique ORDER BY keys
Computing running totals in app code row-by-row

lessons.title: Top-N per group and deduplication patterns
concepts: Top-N per group = ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE + filter rn <= N. It handles ties deterministically when the ORDER BY is unique.
Deduplication: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY the-dedupe-key ORDER BY preferred-row-first) then DELETE/keep rn = 1.
NTILE(n) buckets rows into n roughly equal groups — quartiles, deciles for cohort analysis; buckets differ by at most one row.
Prefer one window pass over repeated TOP 1 correlated subqueries: the window version scans once and the plan is usually a single sort.

example.code:
-- Keep the newest row per (customer_id, email) duplicate key
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id, email ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM contacts)
DELETE FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: duplicates share a partition; newest wins rn = 1; the DELETE targets the CTE and removes the losers. ORDER BY updated_at DESC encodes 'keep the freshest' as the tie-break rule.

pitfalls: Correlated TOP 1 subqueries instead of one window pass
Non-unique ORDER BY making 'which row survives' random
NTILE on tiny sets expecting exactly equal buckets

lessons.title: Variables, batches, and control flow
concepts: T-SQL batches are separated by GO (a client directive, not a statement). Variables live for one batch: DECLARE @x INT; SET @x = 5;
SET assigns one variable; SELECT can assign several at once (SELECT @a = col1, @b = col2 FROM ...) — but silently keeps old values when no row matches.
IF/ELSE, WHILE, and TRY/CATCH give procedural control, but reach for them only where set-based SQL can't express the logic (row-by-row is a last resort).
PRINT is for debugging; RETURN exits a procedure with a status code; THROW re-raises errors with context.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the variable computes the cutoff once; EXISTS short-circuits; IF/ELSE branches on it. Variables also make scripts re-runnable by changing one value at the top.

pitfalls: Using GO inside stored procedures (not allowed)
SELECT-assignment silently keeping stale values on no-match
WHILE loops where a single UPDATE would do

lessons.title: Stored procedures: parameters and safe patterns
concepts: Procedures encapsulate logic with parameters: CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetOrders @status VARCHAR(20), @since DATE AS ... — defaults make parameters optional.
OUTPUT parameters return scalar values; result sets return rows — pick result sets for data, OUTPUT for status/counts.
SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses 'N rows affected' chatter that confuses drivers and ORMs. Schema-qualify names (dbo.Proc) to avoid resolution bugs.
Dynamic SQL inside procedures needs sp_executesql with parameters — never concatenate user input (injection), and parameterize for plan reuse.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: default makes @status optional; the result set streams the rows; @count returns the row count via @@ROWCOUNT captured immediately. Callers get data + metadata in one round trip.

pitfalls: Concatenating parameters into dynamic SQL strings
Forgetting SET NOCOUNT ON and breaking ORM mappings
Not schema-qualifying procedure names

lessons.title: Functions: scalar, inline table-valued, and their costs
concepts: Inline table-valued functions (single RETURN SELECT) are macros the optimizer can fold into the plan — usually safe and fast.
Scalar functions and multi-statement TVFs are plan poison: scalar UDFs force row-by-row evaluation (pre-2019), multi-statement TVFs hide cardinality (estimated 1 row... actually 100 pre-2019).
SQL Server 2019+ inlines eligible scalar UDFs, but keep functions simple and deterministic to stay inlinable.
Rule of thumb: business logic that filters/transforms sets → inline TVF or view; per-row formatting → scalar function only if inlinable, else compute in the query.

example.code:
-- Inline TVF: optimizer-friendly
CREATE FUNCTION dbo.fn_RecentOrders(@days INT)
RETURNS TABLE
AS RETURN (
  SELECT id, total FROM orders
  WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(day, -@days, GETDATE()));
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: single-statement RETURN makes it inline — the optimizer merges it into the calling query's plan as if you'd written the SELECT directly. Call it with SELECT * FROM dbo.fn_RecentOrders(30).

pitfalls: Scalar UDF in a WHERE clause over millions of rows
Multi-statement TVF in a hot join path
Assuming 2019+ inlining fixes every UDF (it has eligibility rules)

lessons.title: Error handling: TRY/CATCH and transaction safety
concepts: TRY/CATCH captures runtime errors: in CATCH, ERROR_MESSAGE()/ERROR_NUMBER() log diagnostics; THROW re-raises to the caller.
Pair with transactions: BEGIN TRY > BEGIN TRAN > work > COMMIT; CATCH > IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK > THROW. Never leave a transaction open on error.
SET XACT_ABORT ON makes most errors abort the batch and roll back — the safe default for procedures that write data.
Validate before writing: check preconditions (row exists, status allows transition) and raise meaningful errors instead of letting constraints fire cryptically.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: both updates succeed or neither does. On any error, CATCH rolls back the partial work and THROW preserves the original error for the caller — no silent half-transfers, no orphaned open transactions.

pitfalls: CATCH without ROLLBACK leaving transactions open
CATCH that swallows the error (no THROW, no log)
Forgetting XACT_ABORT ON for multi-statement writes

lessons.title: Reading execution plans: the 5-minute triage
concepts: Get the actual plan (not estimated) for the real parameter values — estimated plans lie when statistics or sniffed parameters differ.
Read right-to-left, top-to-bottom: data flows from the rightmost operators. Highest-cost operators and thick arrows (many rows) are your suspects.
Scans aren't automatically evil: a clustered index scan over most of a small table is fine. The red flags are scans where a seek was expected, and huge gaps between estimated and actual rows.
Key lookups multiply cost per row: a nonclustered seek + lookup per row is fine for 100 rows, deadly for 10M. Covering indexes eliminate them.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: STATISTICS IO shows logical reads per table (the real cost metric); TIME shows CPU/elapsed. Compare reads before and after each tuning change — reads don't lie, duration can (cache warmth).

pitfalls: Tuning from the estimated plan with atypical parameters
Treating every scan as a bug
Optimizing duration without checking logical reads
