lessons.title: Sargability: writing predicates the engine can seek
concepts: Sargable predicates let the engine seek an index: WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'. Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR(order_date) = 2026) forces a scan.
Rewrite function-wrapped predicates as ranges: DATEPART/month/year filters become >= first-day AND < first-of-next-month.
Implicit conversions are silent scan-forcers: comparing a VARCHAR column to an INT literal converts the column (not the literal) — match types exactly.
Leading-wildcard LIKE ('%term') can't seek a B-tree; keep the literal prefix sargable ('term%') or move to full-text indexing.

example.code:
-- Non-sargable vs sargable: same logic, different plan
-- Bad:  WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2026          -- scan
-- Good: WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
--         AND order_date <  '2027-01-01'        -- seek
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the range form preserves the column bare so the engine can seek the date index directly to 2026's slice. Same rows, orders of magnitude fewer reads on large tables.

pitfalls: Functions on indexed columns in WHERE/JOIN
Implicit int/varchar conversions on join/filter columns
LIKE '%...%' expecting index seeks

lessons.title: Statistics and cardinality: why the optimizer picks badly
concepts: The optimizer chooses plans from statistics (data distribution histograms). Stale stats → wrong row estimates → wrong plan (nested loops over 10M rows).
Symptoms of stale stats: a plan that was fast is suddenly slow after bulk loads; estimated vs actual rows differ by orders of magnitude.
Fix: UPDATE STATISTICS on churning tables; consider FULLSCAN for critical ones. Auto-update exists but its thresholds can lag on huge tables.

Parameter sniffing is statistics-adjacent: the plan is compiled for the first parameter value seen; atypical later values reuse a bad plan. Mitigations: OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR, or plan guides.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: after bulk loads, histograms describe yesterday's data. FULLSCAN rebuilds them exactly; re-running shows whether the plan flips to the sane shape. If it does, schedule regular updates.

pitfalls: Rebuilding indexes to fix what is actually a stats problem
Assuming auto-update stats keeps up on billion-row tables
Adding hints before checking statistics freshness

lessons.title: The query-tuning workflow: measure, hypothesize, verify
concepts: Baseline first: capture logical reads, CPU, elapsed, and the actual plan before changing anything. No baseline, no proof of improvement.
Change one thing at a time: one index, one rewrite, one stats update — then re-measure. Compound changes make cause and effect unknowable.
Prefer correctness-preserving changes in order: fix sargability and types (free), update stats (cheap), add/adjust indexes (moderate), rewrite query (careful), hints (last resort).
Verify under production-like conditions: cold cache, representative parameters, concurrent load. A fix that only helps on a warm cache isn't a fix.

example.code:
-- Tuning loop template
-- 1. SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON; capture actual plan  (baseline)
-- 2. Hypothesize: 'scan on orders.order_date ‒ missing index'
-- 3. CREATE INDEX ix_orders_date ON orders(order_date);
-- 4. Re-run: compare reads + plan  (verify)
-- 5. Keep or DROP based on evidence
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the loop is the scientific method applied to queries. Document each iteration's reads; if step 4 doesn't improve, revert — unused indexes tax every write.

pitfalls: Changing three things and declaring victory
Tuning on a warm cache with one hand-picked parameter
Keeping an index that didn't help ('might help later')

lessons.title: B-tree indexes: how seeks actually work
concepts: A B-tree index is a sorted structure over key columns: seeks walk the tree to the first matching key then scan the leaf range — O(log n) to start, sequential after.
The clustered index defines the table's physical order (one per table); nonclustered indexes are separate structures pointing back via the clustering key.
Index keys should be narrow, stable, and ever-increasing where possible: wide keys bloat every nonclustered index (they carry the clustering key).
Choose the clustered key deliberately: identity ints are the default for good reason; GUIDs fragment; wide strings waste space everywhere.

example.code:
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_date
  ON orders (customer_id, order_date);
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: seeks for a customer's orders land directly on that customer's key range, then read order_date in order — both the filter and a date sort are served by one structure.

pitfalls: Indexing every column individually instead of designing composites
GUID clustered keys on insert-heavy tables
Assuming an index helps without checking the plan

lessons.title: Composite index column order
concepts: Order by selectivity AND query pattern: equality columns first, then range/sort columns. (customer_id, order_date) serves 'customer + date range'; reversed, it serves neither well.
Left-most prefix rule: an index on (a,b,c) serves queries on a, (a,b), (a,b,c) — but not on b alone or c alone.
Put the most selective equality column first when queries always filter it; when queries vary, design for the dominant workload and verify with the plan.
Sort direction matters for ORDER BY ... DESC or mixed directions: match the index key order to the query's sort to avoid a sort operator.

example.code:
-- Serves: WHERE customer_id=@c AND order_date BETWEEN ... ORDER BY order_date
CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (customer_id, order_date DESC);
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: customer_id equality seeks to one customer's slice; order_date range narrows within it; DESC matches the ORDER BY so rows stream out pre-sorted. Flip the columns and the seek degrades.

pitfalls: Reversed column order vs the query pattern
One giant index 'covering everything' instead of targeted ones
Ignoring sort direction in the key definition

lessons.title: Covering indexes and INCLUDE
concepts: A covering index contains every column the query needs: the plan never touches the table (no key lookups) — the fastest possible access path.
INCLUDE adds non-key columns to the leaf level: they don't affect key order or seekability but they cover SELECT lists. Prefer INCLUDE over widening keys.
Covering is a trade: wider indexes cost more on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and use more memory. Cover hot read queries; don't cover everything.
Filtered indexes (WHERE status='open') cover a subset: smaller, faster to maintain, perfect for queries that always filter the same predicate.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: a query selecting total/status for a customer+date range is fully served from the index leaf — zero table access. INCLUDE keeps keys narrow (seekable) while covering the SELECT list.

pitfalls: Putting every column in the key instead of INCLUDE
Covering indexes on write-heavy tables without measuring write cost
Missing filtered indexes for always-filtered hot queries

lessons.title: Sargability revisited: index-friendly predicates
concepts: An index only helps predicates the engine can seek: bare column on one side, compatible types, no leading wildcards, no function wrapping.
OR across different columns often defeats seeks (two seeks + concat is possible but not guaranteed); UNION ALL of two seekable queries is the reliable rewrite.
Careful with data types in parameters: a NVARCHAR parameter against a VARCHAR column converts the column — declare parameters with matching types.
Computed/persisted columns can be indexed: persist the expression (e.g., UPPER(email)) and index it when queries always filter the computed form.

example.code:
-- Seekable rewrite of an OR across two indexed columns
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = @c
UNION ALL
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE sales_rep_id = @c;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: each branch seeks its own index; UNION ALL concatenates without a dedupe sort (a customer is rarely also the rep; add dedupe only if overlap is possible). More reliable than hoping the optimizer builds a concat plan.

pitfalls: OR across columns expecting two seeks
NVARCHAR parameters vs VARCHAR columns (silent conversion)
Function-wrapped columns in JOIN predicates

lessons.title: Index maintenance: fragmentation and fill factor
concepts: Fragmentation (out-of-order pages) hurts range scans; page splits (inserts into full pages) cause it. Sequential keys (identity) barely fragment; random keys (GUIDs) fragment fast.
REORGANIZE defragments lightly online; REBUILD recreates the index (can be online in Enterprise). Don't rebuild on a schedule blindly — act on measured fragmentation.
FILLFACTOR reserves free space per page for future inserts: lower values reduce splits on random-insert indexes at the cost of larger indexes.
Monitor with sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats; automate maintenance by fragmentation thresholds, not by calendar superstition.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: fragmentation % is only actionable with enough pages (small indexes: ignore). High fragmentation + many pages + scan-heavy workload → REBUILD; moderate → REORGANIZE. Measure, then act.

pitfalls: Nightly rebuilds of every index regardless of need
Rebuilding tiny indexes (wasted work, no benefit)
Ignoring FILLFACTOR on random-key insert-heavy tables

lessons.title: ACID: what the database promises
concepts: Atomicity: all-or-nothing — a crashed mid-transfer transfer leaves no half-moves. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work. Durability: committed = survives crashes.
Transactions are the unit of correctness: wrap every multi-statement write that must succeed or fail together in BEGIN/COMMIT.
Keep transactions short: the longer a transaction lives, the longer it holds locks and blocks others. Fetch user input before BEGIN, never during.
Single statements are implicitly transactional — the danger zone is multi-statement business operations (debit + credit, order + inventory).

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: both updates are one atomic unit. A crash between them rolls back the debit — money is never created or destroyed. Without the transaction, a crash means $100 vanishes.

pitfalls: Multi-statement writes without explicit transactions
Holding transactions open across user interaction
Assuming single statements need no thought (they're atomic, but business ops span statements)

lessons.title: Isolation levels: choosing your consistency
concepts: READ COMMITTED (default): no dirty reads; but non-repeatable reads and phantoms are possible — fine for most OLTP, wrong for 'read then decide' logic.
REPEATABLE READ: locks read rows till commit (no non-repeatable reads); phantoms still possible; higher blocking.
SERIALIZABLE: full isolation via range locks — correct but deadlock-prone; reserve for critical sections (inventory decrement).
SNAPSHOT: readers see a committed snapshot, writers don't block readers — great for reporting, but writers can hit update conflicts; enable version store first.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: SERIALIZABLE holds the range lock from SELECT to COMMIT, so two concurrent checkouts can't both see qty=1 and both succeed. The AND qty >= @n guard makes oversell impossible even if logic races.

pitfalls: Default isolation for read-then-write business logic
SERIALIZABLE everywhere (deadlock storm)
SNAPSHOT without understanding update conflicts

lessons.title: Locking, blocking, and deadlocks
concepts: Locks are how isolation is enforced: shared (reads), exclusive (writes), and their granularities (row/page/table). Blocking is normal; excessive blocking is a design smell.
Deadlock = cycle: T1 locks A waits for B, T2 locks B waits for A. The engine picks a victim and rolls it back — your code must retry victims, not crash.
Prevention: access tables in the same order everywhere, keep transactions short, use the lowest isolation that stays correct, prefer row-level operations.
Diagnose with the deadlock graph (XML): it shows the exact resources and statements in the cycle — fix the access pattern, not the victim.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: only error 1205 (deadlock victim) retries; anything else re-throws immediately. Bounded retries prevent infinite loops. The real fix is still consistent access order — retries just make victims survivable.

pitfalls: No retry logic on deadlock victims
Fixing deadlocks by killing processes instead of access order
Escalating to table locks 'to be safe'

lessons.title: Optimistic concurrency: rowversion patterns
concepts: Pessimistic locking blocks readers/writers; optimistic concurrency lets everyone proceed and checks at write time — ideal for low-contention edits (user profiles, documents).
Pattern: read row + rowversion; on save, UPDATE ... WHERE id=@id AND rowversion=@rv; if @@ROWCOUNT=0, someone changed it — reload and ask the user to merge.
rowversion is database-wide auto-incrementing binary — perfect for change detection, meaningless as a timestamp.
Choose by contention: high-contention counters → atomic UPDATE (qty = qty - 1); low-contention user edits → optimistic check.

example.code:
-- Optimistic save: only writes if nobody touched the row
UPDATE documents
SET body = @body
WHERE id = @id AND rowversion = @rv;
-- @@ROWCOUNT = 0 → conflict: reload, show diff, let user merge
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: no locks held while the user edits (minutes). The WHERE clause is the entire concurrency control — last-writer-wins becomes explicit-conflict instead of silent overwrite.

pitfalls: Last-writer-wins silent overwrites on shared records
Holding locks while users think
Using datetime 'last modified' instead of rowversion for conflict checks

lessons.title: Transaction design: batching and error strategy
concepts: Batch large writes: one giant transaction holds locks forever and balloons the log — commit in chunks (e.g., 5,000 rows) with a restartable watermark.
Idempotent batches survive restarts: watermark on processed keys so a crashed batch resumes instead of duplicating.
Savepoints allow partial rollback: SAVE TRAN sp1 before a risky step; ROLLBACK TRAN sp1 undoes just that step inside the larger transaction.
Never catch-and-continue past a data error inside a transaction without understanding XACT_STATE: some errors doom the transaction (uncommittable) — check before proceeding.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: 5,000-row chunks keep each transaction short (locks released, log reusable). The migrated flag is the watermark — crash mid-loop and the next run continues where it stopped, no duplicates.

pitfalls: One transaction for a million-row migration
No watermark: restart reprocesses everything
Continuing after an error that doomed the transaction

lessons.title: Least privilege: roles and the access model
concepts: Least privilege: every login gets only the permissions its job needs — no db_owner for applications, no direct table access when procedures suffice.
Roles (not users) own permissions: create app_read, app_write roles, grant to roles, add logins to roles. People change; roles don't.
Ownership chaining: a procedure owned by dbo accessing dbo tables needs no per-table grants for callers — grant EXECUTE only, and the procedure is the security boundary.
Separate duties: the deployment login can alter schema; the app login can only execute procedures and read views. A compromised app can't drop tables.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: permissions attach to roles, users attach to roles. Auditing one role definition beats auditing fifty user grants, and PlaceOrder's EXECUTE-only grant keeps the app off raw tables.

pitfalls: Application logins as db_owner 'to avoid permission errors'
Granting permissions directly to users instead of roles
One super-login shared by app, jobs, and humans

lessons.title: GRANT, REVOKE, DENY: the permission verbs
concepts: GRANT gives, REVOKE removes a grant, DENY explicitly forbids — and DENY beats GRANT (a user in two roles, one denied, is denied).
Permissions are securable-specific: SELECT on a view doesn't imply SELECT on its base tables (that's what ownership chaining is for).
WITH GRANT OPTION lets grantees re-grant — powerful and dangerous; audit who holds it.
Review effective permissions regularly: sys.database_permissions + role memberships show what a login can actually do, not what you think it can.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: DENY is the emergency brake — it wins over all GRANTs. Use it sparingly and document why; a forgotten DENY causes baffling 'permission denied' tickets months later.

pitfalls: REVOKE when you meant DENY (and vice versa)
WITH GRANT OPTION scattered without inventory
Never reviewing effective permissions after role changes

lessons.title: SQL injection: the eternal vulnerability
concepts: Injection happens when input becomes code: string-concatenated SQL. The fix is structural, not filtering: parameterized queries separate code from data, always.
Stored procedures help only if they use parameters internally — a procedure that concatenates parameters into EXEC() is still injectable.
ORMs are not automatic immunity: raw query methods with f-string interpolation are just as vulnerable as hand-rolled SQL.
Defense in depth: parameters first, least-privilege logins second (an injected query running as a read-only login can't drop tables), input validation third.

example.code:
-- Vulnerable vs safe (application code)
-- BAD:  f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
-- GOOD: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (name,))
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the parameterized version sends the SQL shape and the value separately — the value can never become syntax. No escaping, no blocklists, no cleverness required.

pitfalls: Blocklists/escaping instead of parameters
Assuming stored procedures are automatically safe
Giving the web login db_owner so injection becomes catastrophic

lessons.title: Row-level security and data masking
concepts: Row-level security filters rows per user automatically: a predicate function (e.g., WHERE SalesRep = USER_NAME()) enforced by a security policy — the app can't forget the filter.
Dynamic data masking hides sensitive columns from unprivileged users (emails show as a***@****) without changing stored data — masking is presentation, not encryption.
Always Encrypted keeps sensitive columns encrypted such that even DBAs see ciphertext; the app holds the keys. Use for PII/credentials-grade data.
Layer them: RLS for who sees which rows, masking for casual exposure, Always Encrypted for data even admins must not read.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: every query against orders — ad hoc, ORM, report — automatically gets the region filter appended. No app code to forget, no bypass via a new tool.

pitfalls: Masking treated as encryption (DBAs still see masked, not encrypted)
RLS predicate functions that scan (keep them sargable)
Forgetting RLS applies to dbo/admin too unless excluded

lessons.title: Auditing: who did what, provably
concepts: Audits answer 'who changed this and when': SQL Server Audit / database audit specs capture logins, DDL, and DML on sensitive tables to tamper-evident logs.
Capture at the right grain: failed logins (intrusion signal), privilege changes (escalation signal), DML on financial tables (fraud signal). Log everything and you'll drown.
Protect the audit trail: write to a separate, append-only store with restricted access — an audit log the DBA can edit is theater.
Complement with application-level audit tables (changed_by, changed_at, old/new values) for business-meaningful history the DB audit can't narrate.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: every UPDATE on the ledger table by anyone is captured with login, timestamp, and statement. The file target keeps it outside the database, harder to tamper with.

pitfalls: Auditing everything (noise buries signal)
Audit logs editable by the people being audited
No application-level history for business context

lessons.title: Normalization: 1NF through BCNF
concepts: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups — one fact per cell. 2NF: every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (no partial dependencies). 3NF: no transitive dependencies (non-key attributes depend only on the key).
BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key — stricter than 3NF, kills the remaining anomalies (e.g., overlapping candidate keys).
Why it matters: normalized schemas make each fact live in exactly one place — updates can't contradict themselves, the classic anomaly killer.
Normalize first, then denormalize deliberately where measured: normalization is the default; denormalization is an optimization with a maintenance cost.

example.code:
-- 3NF violation: customer name stored on every order (update anomaly)
-- Fix: customers(id PK, name), orders(id PK, customer_id FK → customers)
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: with the name on every order row, renaming a customer means updating N rows — miss one and reports contradict. The FK design stores the name once; orders reference it.

pitfalls: Denormalizing before measuring a real problem
Repeating groups (phone1, phone2, phone3 columns)
Transitive dependencies hiding in 'convenient' columns

lessons.title: Keys and constraints: the schema as documentation
concepts: Primary keys: unique, non-null, stable — surrogate identity keys are the pragmatic default; natural keys (SSN, email) change and leak meaning.
Foreign keys enforce referential integrity AND document relationships — the optimizer also uses them (trusted FKs enable better plans and simplifications).
CHECK constraints encode business rules in the schema (balance >= 0, status IN (...)); UNIQUE prevents duplicates the app 'promises' to avoid; NOT NULL makes requiredness explicit.
Name constraints explicitly (CK_orders_total_nonneg) — auto-generated names make deployments and error messages miserable.

example.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL CONSTRAINT CK_orders_total_nonneg CHECK (total >= 0),
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open');
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the PK, FK, CHECK, and NOT NULL together make illegal states unrepresentable — negative totals and orphan orders are rejected at the door, not discovered in reports.

pitfalls: No foreign keys ('the app enforces it')
Auto-generated constraint names
Natural keys as PKs that later change

lessons.title: ER modeling: from requirements to tables
concepts: Model entities (nouns), attributes, and relationships (verbs) first; tables come second. Cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N) determines the structure.
M:N needs a junction table (students—courses → enrollments); 1:N puts the FK on the many side; 1:1 is rare — usually a split for security or optional extension.
Resolve optionality explicitly: can an order exist without a customer? The NULL/NOT NULL on the FK is a business decision, not a technical default.
Validate the model with questions: 'show me all X with no Y' should be expressible; if a requirement needs procedural code to answer, the model is wrong.

example.code:
-- M:N resolved with a junction table carrying relationship attributes
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id INT REFERENCES students(id),
  course_id INT REFERENCES courses(id),
  enrolled_on DATE NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the composite PK prevents duplicate enrollments; enrolled_on lives on the relationship where it belongs. Queries like 'students in course X' are simple joins — no arrays, no CSV columns.

pitfalls: M:N modeled as comma-separated columns
1:1 splits without a reason
Nullable FKs where the business says 'always'

lessons.title: Denormalization: when and how, deliberately
concepts: Denormalize for measured read pain: reporting queries joining 8 tables at dashboard refresh rates, not hypothetical slowness.
Techniques: summary tables (pre-aggregated), cached counts (orders.order_count maintained by trigger/procedure), wide reporting tables fed by ETL.
Every denormalized copy needs a refresh contract: trigger, scheduled job, or application write-through — and a reconciliation check proving it matches source.
Document the tradeoff at the schema: a comment naming the source query it accelerates and the job that refreshes it. Future you will thank present you.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: dashboards read one narrow table instead of aggregating billions of order rows. The comment is the contract: what feeds it, when, and how drift is detected.

pitfalls: Denormalized copies with no refresh job
Triggers maintaining summaries on hot OLTP tables without measuring
Denormalizing before the normalized design is proven slow

lessons.title: Slowly changing dimensions: history done right
concepts: Type 1: overwrite (no history) — for corrections and attributes where history doesn't matter. Type 2: new row per change with effective dates — full history, the warehouse standard.
Type 2 needs: surrogate key, effective_from/effective_to (or current flag), and ETL that closes the old row and opens the new one atomically.
Type 3: keep previous value in an extra column — only for 'current vs previous' needs; anything deeper wants Type 2.
Choose per attribute, not per table: a customer's name might be Type 1 while their segment is Type 2.

example.code:
-- Type 2: query 'as of' any date
SELECT * FROM dim_customer
WHERE customer_nk = @nk
  AND @asof >= eff_from AND @asof < eff_to;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the date predicate picks the version that was current on @asof. Reports are reproducible for any point in time — auditors love this, Type 1 can never do it.

pitfalls: Type 1 where regulators require history
Overlapping effective ranges (broken ETL)
One SCD type for the whole table regardless of attribute needs

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs: hierarchies and graphs
concepts: A recursive CTE has an anchor (base rows) and a recursive member (joins back to the CTE) — the engine iterates until no new rows. Perfect for org charts, BOMs, category trees.
Always include a depth guard (level < 100) and cycle protection; runaway recursion from cyclic data is the classic production incident.
MAXRECURSION (default 100) is a safety net, not a design tool — set it deliberately per query, 0 (unlimited) only with proven-acyclic data.
Prefer recursive CTEs over while-loop tree walks: set-based, parallelizable, and the plan is inspectable.

example.code:
WITH org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS lvl FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.lvl + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
  WHERE o.lvl < 20)
SELECT * FROM org OPTION (MAXRECURSION 50);
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: anchor grabs the CEO; recursion appends each level. The lvl guard plus MAXRECURSION 50 double-protects against cycles. Result: the whole tree in one statement.

pitfalls: No depth guard on user-maintained hierarchies
MAXRECURSION 0 'to be safe'
UNION instead of UNION ALL (dedupe cost per iteration)

lessons.title: PIVOT, UNPIVOT, and conditional aggregation
concepts: PIVOT rotates rows to columns: one row per group, one column per category value. The IN-list must enumerate the values — dynamic pivots need dynamic SQL.
UNPIVOT does the reverse (columns to rows), useful for normalizing wide survey/export tables.
Conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN...)) is often clearer and portable across dialects — prefer it unless the tool demands PIVOT syntax.
Dynamic pivot (unknown categories at design time): build the IN-list from DISTINCT values, execute with sp_executesql — and validate the generated SQL.

example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: yearly totals become columns per region. The inner query projects exactly (group, pivot-col, value) — extra columns in the source silently become extra groupings, the classic PIVOT bug.

pitfalls: Extra columns in the PIVOT source creating phantom groups
Dynamic PIVOT via string concat without validation
PIVOT when conditional aggregation would be clearer

lessons.title: JSON in SQL Server: storage and querying
concepts: Store JSON in NVARCHAR with ISJSON check constraints; SQL Server 2016+ queries it with JSON_VALUE (scalar), JSON_QUERY (object/array), OPENJSON (shred to rows).
JSON_VALUE returns one scalar per path — index it via a persisted computed column when you filter on it often.
OPENJSON with an explicit schema shreds documents into relational rows for joining — the bridge between document payloads and set logic.
Don't model everything as JSON: query-heavy attributes belong in real columns; JSON is for flexible/sparse payloads, not for avoiding modeling.

example.code:
-- Shred order line-items JSON into rows and join
SELECT o.id, li.sku, li.qty
FROM orders o
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(o.items_json)
  WITH (sku VARCHAR(20) '$.sku', qty INT '$.qty') li;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: OPENJSON turns each document's array into rows with a typed schema; CROSS APPLY correlates per order. Result: document data participating in normal joins and aggregations.

pitfalls: JSON_VALUE in WHERE without a computed-column index
Storing everything as JSON to dodge schema design
OPENJSON without WITH (untyped, slow, error-prone)

lessons.title: MERGE and upsert patterns
concepts: MERGE does INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one statement from a source to a target — the atomic upsert for ETL syncs.
Match on a stable key; WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. Add WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE for deletes carefully — it's a loaded gun on partial sources.
MERGE has edge-case bugs (race conditions without HOLDLOCK); the safe pattern adds WITH (HOLDLOCK) on the target or uses separate UPDATE/INSERT in a transaction.
OUTPUT clause captures what MERGE did ($action, inserted.*, deleted.*) — audit trail for every sync run.

example.code:
MERGE dbo.dim_product WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS t
USING staging_product AS s ON t.nk = s.nk
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (nk, name) VALUES (s.nk, s.name)
OUTPUT $action, inserted.nk;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: HOLDLOCK serializes the key range so concurrent MERGEs can't both insert the same key (the classic race). OUTPUT logs every action for the ETL audit.

pitfalls: MERGE without HOLDLOCK under concurrency
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE on a partial feed
No OUTPUT audit on production syncs

lessons.title: Gaps and islands: the classic analytic pattern
concepts: Gaps-and-islands groups consecutive sequences (dates, ids) into 'islands': subtract a row-number from the sequence value — constant difference = same island.
Steps: order the sequence, compute ROW_NUMBER() over it, group by (value - rn). Each group is one contiguous island with MIN/MAX boundaries.
Applications: consecutive active days, sessionization (events within N minutes), inventory coverage periods, streak detection.
Sessionization variant: LAG to detect gaps > threshold, running SUM of gap flags as session id — same idea, time-based.

example.code:
-- Find consecutive login-day streaks per user
WITH s AS (
  SELECT user_id, login_date,
    DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date), login_date) AS grp
  FROM logins)
SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
  COUNT(*) AS days FROM s GROUP BY user_id, grp;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: for consecutive dates, login_date minus row-number is constant — that constant labels the island. Group by it and MIN/MAX give each streak's boundaries. One pass, no loops.

pitfalls: Looping in app code for streak detection
Forgetting to partition by the entity (user)
Date arithmetic that breaks across month boundaries

lessons.title: Capstone part 1: design the database
concepts: Project: build 'ShopDB' — customers, products, orders, line items — from requirements to a normalized, constrained schema. This is the artifact interviewers ask to whiteboard.
Deliverable 1: ER sketch with cardinalities (customer 1:N orders, order M:N products via line_items). Deliverable 2: DDL with PKs, FKs, CHECKs, defaults, and named constraints.
Apply the modeling domain: 3NF, surrogate keys, junction table for M:N, NOT NULL where the business says 'always'.
Seed it with realistic volume (10k customers, 100k orders) — toy 10-row tables hide every performance lesson.

example.code:
-- Capstone DDL starter (extend to full schema)
CREATE TABLE line_items (
  order_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  qty INT NOT NULL CONSTRAINT CK_li_qty_pos CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id));
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the junction table carries relationship attributes (qty, price-at-purchase — price history matters). Composite PK prevents duplicate line items. Your job: complete customers/products/orders with the same rigor.

pitfalls: Starting queries before the schema is solid
10-row seed data hiding all real behavior
Unnamed constraints you'll regret at deploy time

lessons.title: Capstone part 2: query, index, and tune
concepts: Deliverable: a 10-query workload covering the interview greatest-hits — latest order per customer, running revenue, top products per category, monthly cohorts, streak detection.
For each query: write it, capture the actual plan + logical reads, then design indexes (composite order, INCLUDE, filtered) and re-measure. Document before/after reads.
Include one transaction design (checkout: decrement inventory + create order atomically) with isolation analysis, and one security pass (roles, parameterized access).
Grading rubric: every query sargable, every hot path covered by an index, every multi-statement write transactional, plans showing seeks not scans.

example.code:
-- Capstone tuning log template
-- Q3: top product per category
-- baseline: 48,210 reads, clustered index scan
-- fix: CREATE INDEX ix_p_cat_sales ON products(category_id, sales DESC)
-- after: 312 reads, index seek. Kept: yes.
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: the log is the deliverable as much as the queries — it proves you can diagnose and verify, not just write SQL. Interviewers light up at before/after numbers.

pitfalls: Declaring victory without before/after measurements
Indexing without checking the plan changed
Skipping the transaction/security deliverables

lessons.title: Capstone part 3: review, harden, present
concepts: Harden: run the security checklist — least-privilege roles, no dynamic SQL concat, RLS/masking where PII appears, audit spec on financial tables.
Review: re-read every query for the classic traps — NOT IN with NULLs, outer-join filters in WHERE, fan-out SUMs, non-deterministic TOP. Fix and note each one found.
Present: a 10-minute walkthrough — schema diagram, 3 hardest queries with plans, one tuning win with numbers, transaction design, security model. This is your interview story.
Ship the repo: DDL, seed scripts, queries, tuning log, and a README narrating decisions. A portfolio artifact beats a certificate line.

example.code:
-- Final review query: find any fan-out risk in your own schema
SELECT t.name AS table_name, COUNT(fk.name) AS fk_count
FROM sys.tables t LEFT JOIN sys.foreign_keys fk ON fk.parent_object_id = t.object_id
GROUP BY t.name;
example.walkthrough: Walkthrough: inventory your relationships before presenting — every FK is a potential fan-out in aggregations. Knowing your schema's join graph cold is what makes the whiteboard session effortless.

pitfalls: Presenting syntax instead of decisions and tradeoffs
No README — the repo doesn't explain itself
Skipping the security pass 'because it's a demo'

sections.heading: Queries
items: Logical query order — sQL's logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > @last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n) is stable under churn and faster on deep pages (no scanning skipped rows).
Alias scope — WHERE executes before the SELECT list, so the alias doesn't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after, so it does.
OFFSET/FETCH — is simple and fine for static data.
Common trap — use = instead of LIKE for patterns.
Common trap — use the alias in GROUP BY instead.
Common trap — order doesn't matter for pages.
Common trap — they are identical; UNION is shorter to type.
OFFSET counts rows from the current result start — concurrent inserts/deletes shift everything, causing duplicates/skips across pages. Choose by data volatility.

sections.heading: Aggregations
items: GROUP BY grain — aggregation grain must match the question's grain: order_lines has one row per line item, so COUNT(*) counts lines, not orders. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY computes them.

Aggregation correctness — the #1 aggregation bug is grouping at the wrong grain — always ask 'what is one row here?' before trusting a COUNT. Conditional aggregation puts CASE inside the aggregate — one scan produces all three columns.
Aggregates and NULLs — all aggregates except COUNT(*) skip NULLs: AVG(5, NULL, NULL) = 5, not 1.67. (COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULLs — usually what you want for 'unique'.).

GROUPING SETS lists multiple groupings computed in one pass — ((region,quarter),(region),()) gives detail rows, region subtotals, and the grand total. WHERE filters input rows before grouping — aggregates don't exist yet.
ROLLUP — ROLLUP(region, quarter) gives the hierarchical chain; CUBE gives all combinations.
Common trap — conditional aggregation requires dynamic SQL.
Common trap — add more columns to GROUP BY until the numbers look right.
Common trap — GROUP BY with multiple columns gives subtotals automatically.
Common trap — the query is wrong; averages can't use NULLs at all.

Aggregation grain must match the question's grain — order_lines has one row per line item, so COUNT(*) counts lines, not orders. Fix: COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), or aggregate orders (one row per order) instead.

sections.heading: Joins
items: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows, extending missing matches with NULLs — but WHERE o.status='shipped' then rejects those NULL rows (UNKNOWN ≠ TRUE), silently converting the outer join to an inner join. LEFT JOIN preserves top-level rows with no manager (NULL manager name).
Predicate placement — NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe (correlated predicate per row) and short-circuits.
Fanout — whenever totals look multiplied, check join fanout first.

Join grain — FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched pairs plus unmatched rows from both sides (NULLs where the other side is missing) — the reconciliation shape in one query. A self join aliases the table twice (e, m) so it plays both roles: employee row and manager row.
Anti-joins — rule: for anti-joins, NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN/IS NULL; treat NOT IN as guilty until proven NULL-free.
Common trap — fanout only happens with FULL JOIN.
Common trap — LEFT JOIN is broken in SQL Server.
Common trap — self joins require temp tables.
Common trap — UNION of two LEFT JOINs.
NOT IN — NOT IN (subquery with NULL) → every comparison is UNKNOWN → zero rows. WHERE right.id IS NULL is equivalent and sometimes clearer.

sections.heading: Window Functions
items: ROW_NUMBER — ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows within each department; the outer filter rn=1 keeps each department's top earner with all columns. ROW_NUMBER: 1,2,3 — unique, arbitrary among ties.
PARTITION BY — lAG(expr) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY day) returns the previous row's value within each product's timeline — no self-join, no date arithmetic, handles gaps naturally.
Top-N per group — GROUP BY + MAX needs a self-join to recover the row. GROUP BY is for collapsing; OVER() is for annotating.

Window frames — the default window frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — RANGE treats tied ORDER BY values as peers, giving them identical results. That's the window function superpower: aggregates at any grain alongside detail rows.
ROWS vs RANGE — know your frame: ROWS = physical, RANGE = logical peers.
Common trap — window functions require GROUP BY.
Common trap — GROUP BY dept with MAX(salary).
Common trap — GROUP BY with the average joined back.
Common trap — LAST_VALUE works with the default frame.

sections.heading: T-SQL Programming
items: TRY/CATCH + explicit transaction — on error, CATCH rolls back the open transaction (@@TRANCOUNT check) and THROW re-raises the original error with its number/line — the caller gets truth, not a masked message.
Transaction control — SET XACT_ABORT ON makes most runtime errors abort the batch and roll back the transaction — fail-atomic instead of fail-partial. Never leave a transaction half-committed.
Temp tables — functions: callable inline in queries, must be side-effect-free (no DML on base tables, deterministic preferred) — perfect for 'calculate discount'.
Common trap — NOCOUNT breaks result sets.
Common trap — use functions for ETL workflows.
Common trap — @@ERROR checks after every statement.

Statistics — estimated vs actual row counts: a big gap = the optimizer decided on bad cardinality — usually stale/missing statistics (UPDATE STATISTICS) or skewed data needing filtered stats.
Plan caching — a single set-based UPDATE...FROM processes all rows in one plan, one pass. The plan names the operators (seek vs scan, loop vs hash vs merge join); the row-count gap names the cause.
